decisions.title: Programme length and phase structure
decisions.context: You have never trained and want everything from hypertrophy and fat loss to VO₂max and balance. Too short a plan stops just as muscle growth gets going; too complex a plan asks for decisions you cannot yet calibrate. The structure sets when new elements arrive and when you reassess.

options.name: One-year programme in five phases, then repeating cycles
options.summary: P0 Orientation (1 week); P1 Foundations (12 weeks, full-body); P2 Development (16 weeks, upper/lower); P3 Athletic (24 weeks, three 8-week emphasis blocks); then repeating 12-week P4 cycles, plus an optional Maintenance mode.
options.for: With volume equated, the [[term:periodisation|periodisation]] model does not change [[term:hypertrophy|hypertrophy]] (ES 0.13), and in untrained people linear and undulating models give the same [[term:1rm|1RM]] gain (ES 0.06) [@Moesgaard2022_periodization], so phases can add volume, skills and conditioning when they become useful. Fibre growth becomes measurable only after several weeks [@Damas2016_JPhysiol_MyoPS] and strength gains decelerate over years in competitive lifters [@Latella2024_longTermStrength]. In one 6-week trial in inactive students, support for variety improved adherence slightly (partial eta-squared 0.05) [@Sylvester2015_varietySupportRCT].
options.against: Phase lengths are pragmatic, untested choices (inference). Habit formation took a median of about two months [@Singh2024_habitFormationTime], so early changes could unsettle a routine that is still forming.

options.name: A single 8-12-week novice programme
options.summary: One simple programme, after which you decide what comes next.
options.for: Novices progress on simple training; one very-low-certainty analysis found larger strength effects for non-periodised programmes in untrained young adults (ES 1.72 vs 1.05) [@Polito2021_moderators].
options.against: It ends just as gains become structural (fibre size rose measurably only by week 10) [@Damas2016_JPhysiol_MyoPS] and leaves months 4-12 and your aerobic and athletic goals unplanned.

options.name: An open-ended fixed routine
options.summary: The same sessions indefinitely, adding load whenever possible.
options.for: Linear and daily undulating models give the same hypertrophy (d -0.02) [@Grgic2017_LPvsDUP_hypertrophy].
options.against: Monotony works against your boredom risk; in one small trial in trained men, varied exercise selection raised intrinsic motivation without costing gains [@BazValle2019_variationMotivation], and undulation may help 1RM once you are trained (ES 0.61, CI 0.00 to 1.22) [@Moesgaard2022_periodization].

options.name: Complex periodisation from the start
options.summary: Block or undulating periodisation with planned hypertrophy, strength and power phases from week 1.
options.for: Periodised plans gave larger 1RM gains (ES 0.43), especially in untrained people [@Williams2017_periodization].
options.against: Those comparisons were not consistently volume-equated; with volume equated the 1RM advantage was smaller (ES 0.31) and there was no hypertrophy benefit [@Moesgaard2022_periodization]; in one small trial in trained men, block periodisation gave smaller muscle and bench-press gains (but larger jump gains) than mixed-quality sessions [@Bartolomei2023_blockVsMixed].

decisions.choiceSummary: Run a one-year programme in five phases (P0 1 week, P1 12 weeks full-body, P2 16 weeks upper/lower, P3 24 weeks in three 8-week emphasis blocks), then repeating 12-week P4 cycles, with an optional Maintenance mode.
decisions.rationale:
The phases are not there to produce a periodisation effect. They add complexity in the order you can absorb it: technique and habit in [[phase:p1]], volume, a four-day split, intervals and run-walk in [[phase:p2]], barbell strength, conditioning and athletic work in [[phase:p3]], then a chosen emphasis in each [[phase:p4]] cycle. ACSM's 2026 position stand includes individualising training to maximise adherence in its primary recommendation [@ACSM2026_position_stand].

Each boundary is a reassessment point, which matters because responses vary widely (biceps size changed by -2% to +59% after identical training, a range partly widened by measurement error) [@Hubal2005_variability]. Short breaks may cost little: in one small bench-press trial in untrained men, 3-week breaks between 6-week blocks did not reduce six-month gains [@Ogasawara2013_periodicVsContinuous], hence [[phase:pm]] Maintenance mode. The link between variety and your own adherence is mostly inference.
decisions.confidenceNote: Outcome evidence on periodisation and variability is moderate, and on breaks low (one small trial); the phase lengths and order are pragmatic design choices no trial has tested.
profileData: Never trained: novice adaptations dominate the first months
Goal order: aesthetics and hypertrophy, fat loss, strength and endurance, then athletic qualities
Boredom is the main quit risk
About 60 min at 13:00, before a 16:00-01:00 shift
wouldChange: Sessions missed through boredom (introduce variation sooner)
Progress stalling before week 12 (start Phase 2 earlier)
Long-term novice trials showing one periodisation model improves hypertrophy or adherence
A long busy period or injury (switch to Maintenance mode)

decisions.title: Starting without medical clearance (pre-participation screening)
decisions.context: You are 31, have never trained and report no symptoms, diagnoses or medications. Should a doctor's visit or tests come first, or is a structured self-check enough? A needless barrier delays the start; a missed warning sign matters more when you train alone.

options.name: PAR-Q+ self-check, then a gradual start
options.summary: Complete the PAR-Q+; if every answer is NO, start without medical clearance at light-to-moderate intensity, progress gradually, and seek evaluation if any warning symptom appears.
options.for: ACSM screening rests on current activity, symptoms or known cardiovascular, metabolic or renal disease, and intended intensity; it dropped risk-factor counting because the old process caused excessive referrals that could deter exercise [@Riebe2015_ACSMscreening]. On the PAR-Q+, NO to all seven questions clears you and any YES routes to follow-up [@PARQplusCollab2025_PARQplus]. Of 1,670 people screened this way, all were cleared for maximal exercise and none had an adverse event [@Yee2019_PARQplusBPcutpoints].
options.against: It relies on you recognising symptoms. Vigorous exertion by unfit people transiently raises cardiac risk in susceptible individuals [@Franklin2020_AHAexerciseRisk], so a gradual start is still needed.

options.name: Routine medical examination and ECG first
options.summary: See a doctor and have a resting ECG or exercise test before the first session.
options.for: Could detect rare silent heart disease and reassure you (inference; no catalogued study tests this in asymptomatic novices).
options.against: Guidance does not require routine clearance for asymptomatic adults, and the old process's excessive referrals were judged a possible barrier to exercise [@Riebe2015_ACSMscreening].

options.name: No screening
options.summary: Start training without any health questions.
options.for: Absolute risk at 31 without symptoms is very low (inference), and habitual activity lowers coronary risk overall [@Franklin2020_AHAexerciseRisk].
options.against: Cardiac events are often preceded by warning symptoms [@Riebe2015_ACSMscreening], which is what the few-minute PAR-Q+ asks about [@PARQplusCollab2025_PARQplus].

decisions.choiceSummary: Complete the PAR-Q+ before the first session and, if every answer is NO, start without medical clearance at light-to-moderate intensity, progress gradually, and seek evaluation if any warning symptom appears.
decisions.rationale:
Both the ACSM model and the PAR-Q+ support self-screening without routine referral for people with no symptoms or known disease [@Riebe2015_ACSMscreening; @PARQplusCollab2025_PARQplus], and resistance training is judged safe for adults with and without cardiovascular disease [@Paluch2023_AHAresistanceTraining]. Because you are inactive, the same logic points to a light-to-moderate start (inference from the three factors), which [[phase:p0]] and early [[phase:p1]] provide ([[dec:D07]]).

Residual risk is handled by stop rules rather than tests: chest pain, pressure or discomfort, pain spreading to the jaw, neck, back or arms, unusual breathlessness, or feeling faint means stop at once and call emergency help [@CDC2024_heartAttackSymptoms]. The full list is on [[plan:safety]].
decisions.confidenceNote: Upper end of moderate: two current guidance documents and a 1,670-person screening cohort agree, but no trial has compared screening strategies.

Currently inactive (never trained)
Trains alone, so warning signs must be self-recognised
Resting blood pressure not yet recorded
wouldChange: Any YES answer on the PAR-Q+
A new symptom, diagnosis or medication (re-screen)

decisions.title: Baseline assessment battery
decisions.context: A baseline shows change that the mirror and the scale hide, and each phase boundary needs numbers to reassess against. You train alone, own a consumer [[term:bia|bioelectrical impedance (BIA)]] scale and have no laboratory access, so the tests must be safe solo, cheap and repeatable.

options.name: Field tests plus tape, photos and the weight trend
options.summary: Rockport 1.6 km walk, push-ups, pull-ups, standing broad jump, single-leg stance (each leg, eyes open and closed), fingertip-to-floor, knee-to-wall and resting heart rate, plus girths, photos and the morning weight trend.
options.for: The Rockport walk estimates [[term:vo2max|VO₂max]] with a cross-validated SEE of 0.355 L/min [@Kline1987_Rockport]. Timed push-up and modified pull-up tests had a minimal detectable change of about 2 reps [@Negrete2010_UEtestsMDC], and a soldier test battery including max-rep pull-ups had between-day ICCs of 0.87-0.98 [@Lester2014_pullupReliability]. In back-pain patients, fingertip-to-floor correlated with radiographic trunk flexion (r -0.96) and was highly reliable (ICC 0.99) [@Perret2001_fingertip_floor_test], knee-to-wall has a minimal detectable change of about 1.6-1.9 cm [@Powden2015_WBLT_reliability], and best-of-3 single-leg stance is highly reliable [@Springer2007_unipedalstance]. Each 10 bpm higher resting heart rate is associated with 17% higher all-cause mortality (observational) [@Aune2017_RHRmeta].
options.against: Field estimates are imprecise for one person: a single VO₂max estimate is roughly ±9 mL/kg/min (inference: twice the SEE of about 4.6 mL/kg/min at your weight), and heat and heart-rate error shift it. The broad jump rose 12 cm on retest from learning alone (MDC 29 cm, falling to 1 cm after familiarisation) [@MarinJimenez2024_SLJ].

options.name: Laboratory testing (DXA, gas-analysis VO₂max)
options.summary: Criterion measures of body composition and aerobic capacity.
options.for: Far more accurate for an individual: against DXA, a foot-to-foot scale erred by an RMSE of 5.6 percentage points of body fat in men [@Nana2022_footBIAvsDXA].
options.against: Costly and hard to repeat, while walk/run field tests correlate with measured VO₂max up to r 0.79 [@MayorgaVega2016_walkrunMA], enough to show the direction of change (inference).

options.name: 1RM strength tests
options.summary: Work up to a single maximal lift on the main exercises.
options.for: Precise for the tested lift, whereas predicting [[term:1rm|1RM]] from multi-rep sets has error (SEE about 16 kg for leg press from a 5RM) [@Reynolds2006_1RMprediction].
options.against: Maximal free-weight attempts alone are the riskiest form of testing (inference): in US emergency-department data, two-thirds of weight-training injuries came from weights dropping on the lifter, and 90% involved free weights [@Kerr2010_weightTrainingED]. 1RM gains also largely reflect skill in the tested movement [@Saeterbakken2025_taskSpecificityMeta].

options.name: Use the BIA scale's outputs
options.summary: Body fat, muscle mass, visceral fat and the other numbers the scale displays.
options.for: Convenient and highly repeatable (precision error 0-0.5 percentage points) [@Siedler2022_15BIAdevices].
options.against: Individual accuracy is poor (SEE 3.1-7.5 points), and even for change the devices had SEE 1.7-2.6 points [@Siedler2022_15BIAdevices], similar to or larger than a novice's likely change over months (inference); meals, fluid and timing distort readings [@Tinsley2021_trackingchange].

decisions.choiceSummary: Record a field battery (Rockport walk, push-ups, pull-ups, broad jump, single-leg stance, fingertip-to-floor, knee-to-wall, resting heart rate) plus girths, photos and the weight trend, with no 1RM testing and no use of BIA outputs other than weight.
decisions.rationale:
Every chosen test can be done alone, has published reliability or validity, and maps onto a goal: aerobic fitness, upper-body strength, power, balance, flexibility or shape. Tape, photos and the weight trend cover body composition (photos are an unvalidated, qualitative record; practical convention). Strength is tracked as [[term:e1rm|estimated 1RM]] from logged sets ([[tool:e1rm]]) instead of maximal solo attempts. Fingertip-to-floor was preferred to the more hamstring-specific straight-leg raise, which is also reliable (MDD 6-7 degrees) [@Neto2015_AKE_SLR_reliability] but needs a second person (practical convention).

Your eyes-open stance times (left 20 s, right 30 s) sit well below the 44 s best-of-3 average for men aged 18-39 tested barefoot with arms crossed and a 45-s cap [@Springer2007_unipedalstance], so each leg is tracked ([[dec:D28]]). Treat changes inside a test's noise as no change.
decisions.confidenceNote: Most tests have reasonable reliability data, but several come from soldiers or clinical samples, and none were checked in hot, humid conditions.

decisions.title: Energy strategy for Phase 1: recomposition vs surplus vs deficit
decisions.context: You want visible muscle and less fat, in that order, and you start untrained at about 20% body fat (equations 17-22%, plausible 17-24%) with a navel waist of 86 cm. Eating above, at or below maintenance ([[term:energy-balance|energy balance]]) changes how much of each you get, and how the first months feel.

options.name: Recomposition: maintenance to about -300 kcal/day
options.summary: A smoothed weight trend of 0 to -0.25 kg/week with protein 1.6-2.2 g/kg/day; the target changes per phase by rule.
options.for: [[term:recomposition|Recomposition]] is well documented, including beyond the novice stage, according to a narrative review [@Barakat2020_recomp]. Resistance training alone, without a prescribed diet, lowered body fat by 1.46 percentage points and fat mass by 0.55 kg versus control [@Wewege2022_RTbodyFat]. A deficit reduces lean-mass gain (ES -0.57) but not strength gain, and meta-regression put the deficit that abolishes the average lean gain at roughly 500 kcal/day [@Murphy2022_deficitLeanMass]. In adults under 65, extra protein raised lean-mass gain significantly only in trials reaching 1.6 g/kg/day or more [@Nunes2022_proteinLBM].
options.against: Progress is slow and hard to see, because body-composition methods have errors comparable to the changes studied [@Barakat2020_recomp], and even a small deficit trims lean gain somewhat [@Murphy2022_deficitLeanMass].

options.name: Surplus ('bulk')
options.summary: Eat 5-20% above maintenance to gain about 0.25-0.5% of body weight per week.
options.for: One bodybuilding narrative review suggests a 10-20% surplus for novices [@Iraki2019_offseason], and in one small trial in trained lifters a 15% surplus raised bench-press 1RM more than maintenance [@Helms2023_surplus].
options.against: In that trial, muscle thickness did not differ between maintenance, +5% and +15%, while skinfolds rose with the larger surplus [@Helms2023_surplus]. Fat made up 50% to over 90% of stored excess energy when untrained people were overfed by about 40% [@Bray2012_overfeedingProtein], and the surplus needed for hypertrophy is unknown [@Slater2019_surplus].

options.name: Aggressive deficit (more than 500 kcal/day)
options.summary: Lose 0.5-1% of body weight per week from the start.
options.for: Faster fat loss; with 2.4 g/kg/day protein and intense training, young men gained 1.2 kg lean mass over 4 weeks in a 40% deficit [@Longland2016_highProteinDeficit].
options.against: That trial used a heavy supervised workload; on average, deficits this large abolish lean gain [@Murphy2022_deficitLeanMass]. In one small trial in elite athletes, slower loss (0.7%/week) raised lean mass 2.1% while faster loss did not [@Garthe2011_weightLossRate].

options.name: Strict maintenance
options.summary: Eat at maintenance and let training change body composition.
options.for: Simplest, and recomposition still occurs with training alone [@Wewege2022_RTbodyFat].
options.against: Fat loss is slower, and your waist already exceeds the 78 cm first action level proposed for Asian Indian men in one north Indian study [@Misra2006_IndianWaist], though not the 90 cm consensus threshold.

decisions.choiceSummary: In Phase 1, eat at maintenance while calibration continues in weeks 1-2, then from maintenance to about 300 kcal/day below it from week 3 (weight trend 0 to -0.25 kg/week) with protein 1.6-2.2 g/kg/day, changing the target only by the phase rules.
decisions.rationale:
Hypertrophy ranks above fat loss in your goals, and lean gain is the outcome most sensitive to deficit size, so the deficit is capped well below the ~500 kcal/day average at which lean gain disappears [@Murphy2022_deficitLeanMass]. Your 86 cm waist is above the 78 cm action level proposed in one Indian study [@Misra2006_IndianWaist] (though below the 90 cm consensus threshold), which argues against a surplus; Forbes's relation, derived from diet-only changes without training, also predicts that the fat-free share of weight gain falls as body fat rises [@Hall2007_ForbesPratio].

Success means waist falling or stable while strength and limb girths rise, even if weight is flat (practical convention), tracked with [[tool:energy]] and [[rule:energy-adjustment]]. Later phases switch strategy via [[rule:phase-nutrition]]; protein details are in [[dec:D19]].
decisions.confidenceNote: Meta-analyses support the direction (deficits blunt lean gain; training alone reduces fat), but the cut-offs are between-study averages rather than individual thresholds, and your body-fat estimate is itself uncertain.

decisions.title: Training split and frequency in Phase 1
decisions.context: You have about 60 minutes at 13:00 before work, two cardio sessions to fit on other days, and every lift to learn. The split decides how often each muscle and movement is practised and how much fits into each session.

options.name: Three non-consecutive full-body sessions (A/B)
options.summary: For example Monday, Wednesday and Friday, alternating two templates, so each muscle is trained 2-3 times a week.
options.for: With weekly volume equated, [[term:training-frequency|training frequency]] does not change [[term:hypertrophy|hypertrophy]] [@Schoenfeld2019_frequency_hypertrophy] and had a negligible effect in a large dose-response model [@Pelland2025_volume_frequency]; split and full-body routines give similar results [@RamosCampo2024_split_vs_fullbody], so the layout can follow schedule and adherence. ACSM advises training all major muscles at least twice weekly [@ACSM2026_position_stand]. Without volume equating, more frequent training went with larger multi-joint 1RM gains [@Grgic2018_frequency_strength].
options.against: Session length caps volume, so priority muscles reach 12-16 weekly sets only after a later change of split (inference).

options.name: Two full-body sessions per week
options.summary: Meets the minimum with fewer gym days.
options.for: Meets the ACSM minimum [@ACSM2026_position_stand], and a twice-weekly multi-set prescription ranked top for hypertrophy in a network meta-analysis, although differences between prescriptions were small [@Currier2023_BJSM_NMA].
options.against: Within 60-min sessions, weekly volume tops out near 8-10 sets per muscle, with fewer practice exposures for new lifts (inference).

options.name: Four-day upper/lower split from the start
options.summary: Upper and lower body twice a week each.
options.for: Similar outcomes to full-body at equal volume [@RamosCampo2024_split_vs_fullbody], with more room for volume.
options.against: You do not need that volume yet ([[dec:D06]]), and four lifting days plus two cardio days leave one rest day while the first sessions cause the most muscle damage [@Damas2016_JPhysiol_MyoPS].

options.name: One muscle group per day (once a week each)
options.summary: A classic five-day body-part split.
options.for: With volume equated, frequency did not change hypertrophy [@Schoenfeld2019_frequency_hypertrophy].
options.against: An earlier, smaller meta-analysis favoured twice weekly over once (ES 0.49 vs 0.30) [@Schoenfeld2016_frequency_hypertrophy], although its larger 2019 update found no volume-equated difference [@Schoenfeld2019_frequency_hypertrophy]; it falls below the ACSM minimum [@ACSM2026_position_stand], concentrates soreness and gives each lift one practice exposure a week.

decisions.choiceSummary: In Phase 1, lift three times a week on non-consecutive days, alternating two full-body templates (A/B), so each muscle is trained two to three times a week.
decisions.rationale: Once volume is fixed, frequency and split type barely matter, so the deciding factors are practical: three sessions fit your 13:00 slot, split weekly volume into manageable chunks, and give each new lift two or three practice exposures a week. Rest days between sessions fit the finding that muscle protein synthesis was still raised 48 h after a session in a small tracer study of untrained adults [@Phillips1997_MPS_untrained] (mechanistic reasoning). Cardio goes on non-lifting days ([[dec:D11]]). In [[phase:p2]] the split becomes upper/lower ([[dec:D12]]) because the higher volume no longer fits three 60-min sessions.
decisions.confidenceNote: Upper end of moderate: several meta-analyses agree that frequency and split matter little at equal volume; the practical arguments (skill practice, scheduling) are inference.

About 60 min at 13:00 before a 16:00 shift
Two aerobic sessions per week on non-lifting days
Boredom risk (two alternating templates add variety)
wouldChange: Only two days available (use two longer full-body sessions)
Boredom threatening adherence (start upper/lower sooner)

decisions.title: Weekly volume and how it ramps
decisions.context: Weekly sets per muscle are the main growth dial you control. Too few leave growth on the table; too many early on add soreness and time without adding much, and your 60-min sessions must also hold technique practice and warm-up sets.

options.name: Low start, then a ramp weighted to priority muscles
options.summary: About 4-6 [[term:fractional-sets|fractional sets]] per muscle per week in weeks 1-2 and 8-12 in weeks 3-11; from Phase 2, 12-16 for priority muscles (lateral and rear deltoids, upper chest, back, arms) and 10-13 for legs; 6-8 for maintenance.
options.for: [[term:hypertrophy|Hypertrophy]] rises with weekly volume with diminishing returns, and counting indirect sets as half fitted best [@Pelland2025_volume_frequency]; each extra weekly set was associated with about 0.37 percentage points more growth, with a borderline trend favouring 10+ sets [@Schoenfeld2017_volume_meta]. ACSM supports 10 or more sets per muscle per week [@ACSM2026_position_stand]. A low start suits week 1, when protein synthesis goes mainly to repairing damage rather than growth in a small mechanistic study [@Damas2016_JPhysiol_MyoPS] (mechanistic reasoning).
options.against: The ramp timing is inference, and responses vary: with 3 sets vs 1 set per exercise, only 13 of 34 people showed a clear extra hypertrophy benefit [@Hammarstrom2020_volume_ribosomes].

options.name: High volume (20+ sets) from the start
options.summary: Begin near the top of the dose-response curve.
options.for: The volume slope stays positive at high doses [@Pelland2025_volume_frequency].
options.against: Returns diminish: in trained men 12-20 vs more than 20 weekly sets did not differ for quadriceps or biceps (only triceps favoured more) [@BazValle2022_volume_trained]. Novices already respond to modest doses [@Krieger2010_sets_hypertrophy], and 20+ sets would not fit 60-min sessions.

options.name: Minimal single-set training
options.summary: One hard set per exercise, about 4 sets per muscle per week.
options.for: About 4 weekly sets per muscle is effective and time-efficient [@Iversen2021_time_efficient]; low volume already gives large strength gains [@Ralston2017_volume_strength], and in older adults low volume was the most effective for lean mass [@Radaelli2024_older_volume_NMA].
options.against: Multiple sets gave about 40% larger hypertrophy effects than single sets [@Krieger2010_sets_hypertrophy], and the older-adult finding may not transfer to a 31-year-old.

decisions.choiceSummary: Start at about 4-6 fractional sets per muscle per week, rise to 8-12 from week 3, then 12-16 for priority muscles (legs 10-13) from Phase 2, with 6-8 as the maintenance dose.
decisions.rationale:
The dose-response evidence supports reaching at least 10 weekly sets, not starting there. Weeks 1-2 are for technique and for the [[term:repeated-bout-effect|repeated-bout effect]] to blunt later soreness (inference). From [[phase:p2]], extra sets go where your goal needs them: shoulders, upper chest, back and arms shape an athletic upper body, while legs stay at 10-13 because running and plyometrics add lower-body load later (inference). Synergists count 0.5, so direct arm and lateral deltoid sets are still programmed; in one small trial in untrained men, a direct curl gave about twice the elbow-flexor growth of a row [@Mannarino2021_curl_vs_row].

Because responses vary, volume for a lagging muscle rises only on evidence from your logs and tape ([[rule:lagging-muscle]]). The maintenance dose is covered in [[dec:D18]].
decisions.confidenceNote: Dose-response meta-analyses agree on direction and diminishing returns; the exact set numbers and ramp timing are judgement layered on that evidence.

decisions.title: How close to failure: effort targets for a solo novice
decisions.context: How hard each set is matters as much as how many you do. You train alone, so a failed barbell rep has no spotter, and you have never judged effort, so your early estimates of reps left will be rough.

options.name: Graded RIR targets by exercise type
options.summary: Phase 0 at about 4 and Phase 1 weeks 1-2 at 3-4 [[term:rir|reps in reserve (RIR)]]; then free-weight compound lifts at 2-3 RIR and never to failure, machines at 1-2 RIR, isolation at 0-2 RIR (the last set may reach failure on machines or cables); RIR calibration in Phase 1 weeks 5 and 9 and Phase 2 weeks 2, 7 and 12, then every 4-6 weeks.
options.for: Getting close to failure matters more than reaching it: [[term:momentary-failure|momentary failure]] vs non-failure gave ES 0.12 (CI -0.13 to 0.37) for hypertrophy [@Refalo2023_failure_hypertrophy], failure did not improve strength [@Grgic2022_failure_meta], and non-failure was slightly better for dynamic strength (SMD 0.24) [@Wu2026_nonfailure_meta]. In one small trial in trained men, failure slowed recovery by roughly 24-48 h [@MoranNavarro2017_failure_recovery]. With light loads, effort mattered most in one small trial (30% 1RM not to failure +2.8% vs to failure +7.8%) [@Lasevicius2022_failure_by_load], so isolation and high-rep sets go closer.
options.against: An exploratory meta-regression found hypertrophy keeps rising as sets end closer to failure [@Robinson2024_RIR_metaregression], so a 2-3 RIR margin on compounds may cost a little growth.

options.name: Every set to failure
options.summary: End each set when another rep is impossible.
options.for: Removes guesswork, and in trained subjects failure modestly favoured hypertrophy (ES 0.15) [@Grgic2022_failure_meta].
options.against: In one small trial in trained lifters, sessions felt worse (Feeling Scale +0.3 vs +1.2 with RIR) [@Refalo2025_proximityPerceptual], and most weight-training injuries seen in US emergency departments came from weights dropping on the lifter [@Kerr2010_weightTrainingED], a real risk without a spotter.

options.name: Always stop 3 or more reps short
options.summary: A conservative margin on every set.
options.for: Least fatigue: after sets at 3 RIR, bench-press velocity had fully recovered by 24 h [@Refalo2023_proximityFatigue].
options.against: Possibly less hypertrophy [@Robinson2024_RIR_metaregression], especially for light-load sets [@Lasevicius2022_failure_by_load]; and since people under-predict reps left by about 1 [@Halperin2022_RIR_accuracy], a planned 3 RIR may really be 4 (inference).

options.name: Percentage-of-1RM loading
options.summary: Loads set as fixed percentages of a tested 1RM.
options.for: Autoregulated and percentage loading gave similar 1RM gains (MD 2.07 kg, CI -0.32 to 4.46) [@Hickmott2022_autoregulation].
options.against: Needs a frequently retested [[term:1rm|1RM]], unsafe alone, and one percentage leaves different people at very different RIR [@Pelland2022_RIR_methods].

decisions.choiceSummary: Start at about 4 RIR in Phase 0 and 3-4 RIR in Phase 1 weeks 1-2, then keep free-weight compound lifts at 2-3 RIR and never to failure, machines at 1-2 RIR and isolation at 0-2 RIR (last set may reach failure on machines or cables), with RIR calibration in Phase 1 weeks 5 and 9 and Phase 2 weeks 2, 7 and 12, then every 4-6 weeks.
decisions.rationale:
The evidence points to a non-linear relation: sets must end reasonably close to failure, but reaching it adds little and costs recovery. The graded scheme puts the hardest efforts where failure is safe (machines, cables, isolation) and keeps a margin where a failed rep is dangerous (free-weight compounds without a spotter). The cautious first weeks reflect that vigorous exertion is riskiest for unfit people [@Franklin2020_AHAexerciseRisk] and that exertional rhabdomyolysis, though uncommon, can follow unaccustomed or poorly prescribed exercise [@Rawson2017_exertionalRhabdo].

Novices can use RIR: experience did not clearly change accuracy [@Remmert2023_RIRtrainedUntrained], but errors grow far from failure and in sets above 12 reps [@Halperin2022_RIR_accuracy]. At each calibration (Phase 1 weeks 5 and 9, Phase 2 weeks 2, 7 and 12, then every 4-6 weeks), take the last set of a safe machine exercise to failure and compare with your estimate ([[rule:rir-calibration]]); the routine itself is untested (inference).
decisions.confidenceNote: Meta-analyses agree that failure adds little on average, but most trials used trained or mixed samples; the RIR bands and calibration routine are judgement.

decisions.title: Exercise selection: machines and dumbbells first, barbells later
decisions.context: Which exercises you do shapes where you grow and how safely you can train alone. Your goal is an athletic look led by shoulders, upper chest, back and arms, and you start with no lifting skill.

options.name: Machines, cables and dumbbells first; barbells from Phase 2
options.summary: Mostly machines, cables and dumbbells in Phase 1; barbell squat and Romanian deadlift in Phase 2 inside a rack with [[term:safety-arms|safety arms]]; exercises chosen for loading at long muscle lengths and for aesthetic priorities.
options.for: Free weights and machines gave similar hypertrophy (SMD -0.055, 95% CI -0.40 to 0.29; only 5 hypertrophy trials) [@Haugen2023_freeVsMachineMeta; @HernandezBelmonte2023_freeVsMachineRCT]. In single small trials, specific choices grew target muscles more: seated vs lying leg curls +14% vs +9% hamstrings [@Maeo2021_seatedVsProneCurl]; overhead vs neutral triceps work +28.5% vs +19.6% long head [@Maeo2023_overheadTriceps]; standing vs seated calf raises +12.4% vs +1.7% lateral gastrocnemius [@Kinoshita2023_standingVsSeatedCalf]; incline pressing grew the upper chest 0.62 cm more [@Chaves2020_inclineVsFlat]; full squats grew glutes +6.7% vs +2.2% [@Kubo2019_squatDepth]. Full [[term:rom|range of motion]] beat partial for lower-limb hypertrophy (ES 0.88) [@Pallares2021_ROMmeta].
options.against: Strength is task-specific, so barbell strength lags while barbells wait [@Saeterbakken2025_taskSpecificityMeta]. Pooled across studies, training at long muscle lengths made only trivial differences to regional growth [@Varovic2025_lengthRegionalMeta].

options.name: Barbell-centric novice programme (e.g. 3 x 5 linear progression)
options.summary: A few barbell lifts with load added every session.
options.for: Heavy loads maximise 1RM [@Lopez2021_load_NMA], and free-weight-tested strength improves more with free weights [@Haugen2023_freeVsMachineMeta].
options.against: No hypertrophy advantage [@Haugen2023_freeVsMachineMeta], little direct work for lateral deltoids or arms (inference), and free weights account for most weight-training injuries seen in emergency departments, more often fractures or dislocations [@Kerr2010_weightTrainingED].

options.name: Bodyweight only
options.summary: Push-ups, pull-ups, squats and lunges.
options.for: Light loads built muscle similarly when sets were taken to failure [@Schoenfeld2017_load_meta].
options.against: With 5 push-ups and 3 pull-ups you cannot yet dose rep ranges, lower-body loading is limited (inference), and light-load sets work only close to failure [@Lasevicius2022_failure_by_load].

options.name: Machines only
options.summary: No free weights at any stage.
options.for: Similar hypertrophy in one trial in trained men [@HernandezBelmonte2023_freeVsMachineRCT], and machine injuries were less often fractures or dislocations [@Kerr2010_weightTrainingED].
options.against: Strength transfers poorly between tasks [@Saeterbakken2025_taskSpecificityMeta], and your later strength, power and athletic goals need free-weight skill (inference).

decisions.choiceSummary: Use machines, cables and dumbbells for most Phase 1 work, add the barbell squat and Romanian deadlift in Phase 2 inside a rack with safety arms, and pick exercises for long-length loading and your aesthetic priorities.
decisions.rationale:
Because modality made no clear difference to hypertrophy, safety and learning set the order: machines and dumbbells let a solo novice push sets hard and bail out safely, and barbell skill is added once patterns are stable ([[dec:D15]]). Within each muscle the choices follow the best trials available: [[ex:incline-db-press]] first in the session (strength favours whichever exercise comes first; hypertrophy was unaffected by order) [@Nunes2021_exerciseOrderMeta], [[ex:db-lateral-raise]] or [[ex:cable-lateral-raise]] 2-3 times a week (equal growth) [@Larsen2025_lateralRaiseDBvsCable], [[ex:oh-cable-triceps]], [[ex:seated-leg-curl]], [[ex:standing-calf-raise]] and deep squats ([[ex:goblet-squat]], later [[ex:back-squat]]). Rated upper-body strength explained over 70% of the variance in rated male bodily attractiveness in cross-sectional data [@Sell2017_strengthAttractiveness], which supports the upper-body emphasis but is culturally limited.

The long-length bias is a tie-breaker, not a rule: single trials favour it, the regional meta-analysis finds trivial effects.
decisions.confidenceNote: Modality equivalence rests on one meta-analysis with wide confidence intervals and one trial in trained men; the muscle-specific choices rest mostly on single small trials, and pooled long-length evidence is weaker than those trials suggest.

decisions.title: Progression model: double progression, no formal periodisation in Phase 1
decisions.context: Progression is how the programme keeps asking for slightly more than last time. You need a rule that works without maximal testing, copes with the coarse weight steps of dumbbells and machines, and runs on the data you already log in Hevy.

options.name: Double progression, with structure added later
options.summary: [[term:double-progression|Double progression]]: work within a rep range; when every set reaches the top at the target RIR, add the smallest load step and restart at the bottom. Phase 1 is non-periodised, Phase 2 adds mild daily undulation, Phase 3 uses emphasis blocks, and [[term:deload|deloads]] are planned from Phase 2 (P2 week 8, P3 weeks 8 and 16, P4 week 6) and otherwise triggered by fatigue signals.
options.for: In one small trial in trained lifters, progressing reps at a fixed load and progressing load gave similar hypertrophy and strength (squat 1RM difference 2.0 kg, CI -2.4 to 7.8) [@Plotkin2022_loadVsRepProgression], so a rule combining them is reasonable (inference). ACSM's 2009 novice guidance (now superseded) was to raise load 2-10% once the target is exceeded by 1-2 reps [@ACSM2009_progression_models]. Undulation helped 1RM in trained lifters (ES 0.61) but not untrained ones (ES 0.06), and did not change hypertrophy [@Moesgaard2022_periodization; @Grgic2017_LPvsDUP_hypertrophy].
options.against: No long-term novice trial has tested this exact scheme (inference), and the rule depends on RIR ratings, which err by about 1 rep on average [@Halperin2022_RIR_accuracy].

options.name: Add load every session (linear progression)
options.summary: A fixed increment each time a lift is repeated.
options.for: Simple and plausible early on, when strength gains are fastest (shown in competitive lifters) [@Latella2024_longTermStrength].
options.against: No head-to-head novice data, no built-in rule for when increases must stop, and with light dumbbells one step can be a large percentage jump (inference).

options.name: Percentage-of-1RM programming
options.summary: Sets prescribed as percentages of a tested maximum.
options.for: Gave similar 1RM and muscle-thickness gains to RPE-based loading in trained lifters [@Helms2018_RPEvsPercent].
options.against: Needs a valid, frequently updated [[term:1rm|1RM]], which changes quickly in novices and is risky to test alone, and one percentage yields very different RIR across people [@Pelland2022_RIR_methods].

options.name: Pure RPE autoregulation
options.summary: Choose each day's load by feel, without rep ranges.
options.for: Autoregulated loading matched percentage-based loading for 1RM [@Hickmott2022_autoregulation], with a possible small squat advantage for RPE [@Helms2018_RPEvsPercent].
options.against: Rep-prediction accuracy varied enormously between studies (I² 97.9%) [@Halperin2022_RIR_accuracy], so rep ranges are a useful guard-rail while you learn.

decisions.choiceSummary: Use double progression throughout, keep Phase 1 non-periodised, add mild daily undulation in Phase 2 and emphasis blocks in Phase 3, and take deloads when fatigue signals appear, plus the planned deload weeks from Phase 2 (P2 week 8, P3 weeks 8 and 16, P4 week 6).
decisions.rationale:
Double progression needs no 1RM test, absorbs day-to-day variation in readiness, and turns your Hevy log into a clear prompt: top of the range at the target RIR means add load ([[rule:double-progression]], [[tool:progression]]). Because periodisation does not change hypertrophy and undulation helps strength only in trained lifters, structure arrives once you are past the novice stage, mainly for variety and strength ([[dec:D16]]).

Apart from the planned deload weeks in Phases 2-4, deloads are triggered by stalls, joint irritation or poor recovery ([[rule:stall]], [[rule:deload]]): in one small trial, reduced-volume weeks did not impair hypertrophy in untrained men [@Pancar2026_deloadUntrained], in another a full week off probably left strength slightly lower in trained lifters [@Coleman2024_deloadRCT], and expert consensus frames deloads as fatigue management [@Bell2023_deloadDelphi]. The triggers themselves are judgement, not validated.
decisions.confidenceNote: Progression and periodisation trials are short and mostly in trained or mixed samples; the scheme is consistent with them, but its increments and deload triggers are judgement.

decisions.title: Warm-up and cool-down design (and where stretching goes)
decisions.context: You train at 13:00, an hour after waking, which is early in your biological day, and you cannot touch your toes. The warm-up must prepare you to lift well in limited time; the cool-down is the most reliable slot for the stretching your flexibility goal needs.

options.name: Graded warm-up; stretching after training, for range of motion
options.summary: Warm-up: 6 min easy cardio, dynamic drills, 2 x 30 s single-leg balance per leg (left first) and [[term:ramp-up-sets|ramp-up sets]]. Cool-down: 2 min easy, then [[term:static-stretching|static stretching]] (hamstrings every session, about 5 min per leg per week at about 7/10), aimed at range of motion, not recovery.
options.for: Warming up improved performance in 79% of criteria studied [@Fradkin2010_warmup_performance]; high-load specific warm-ups enhance upper-body strength [@McCrary2015_upperbody_warmup], and in one trial in trained men, warm-up sets near the working load slightly beat a few light reps [@Ribeiro2020_specific_warmup_RT]. Body temperature was the factor most often linked to time-of-day differences, and an extended morning warm-up was judged the best way to reduce them [@Kusumoto2021_diurnal_variation]. Stretch training increases [[term:rom|range of motion (ROM)]] (ES about 1.0) [@Konrad2024_chronic_stretch_ROM], possibly helped by at least about 5 min per week [@Thomas2018_stretch_dose_ROM] (the larger meta-analysis found no clear dose effect [@Konrad2024_chronic_stretch_ROM]) and, in one small calf trial, by higher intensity (6-7/10: +40% vs +15% ROM) [@Nakamura2021_HI_vs_LI_SS]. Balance training reduced sports injuries (RR 0.55) [@Lauersen2014_injury_prevention].
options.against: In one small study in trained men, an extended morning warm-up raised core temperature to evening levels yet did not restore evening lifting performance [@Pullinger2019_morning_warmup_lifts], so the longer cardio may help less than hoped. The routine uses about 10-12 minutes of a 60-min session (inference).

options.name: Static stretching or foam rolling as the warm-up
options.summary: Hold stretches or roll before lifting.
options.for: Short holds cost little (under 30 s: -1.1%) [@Kay2012_acute_static_stretch], and pre-rolling slightly improved flexibility (+4%) [@Wiewelhove2019_foam_rolling_meta].
options.against: Holds of 60 s or more cut maximal strength substantially (ES -0.84) [@Warneke2024_stretch_force_deficit], and neither stretching nor rolling improved acute ROM more than other warm-up activities (ES 0.01) [@Warneke2024_FR_stretch_warmup_ROM].

options.name: No warm-up
options.summary: Start with the first working set.
options.for: Saves several minutes (inference).
options.against: Loses the performance benefit [@Fradkin2010_warmup_performance]; in one small trial in trained people, a general plus specific warm-up gave an 8.4% higher leg-press 1RM than a specific warm-up alone [@Abad2011_general_specific_warmup].

options.name: Long active cool-down for recovery
options.summary: 10-15 min of easy cardio and stretching to speed recovery.
options.for: Speeds blood lactate clearance and may aid cardiovascular recovery [@VanHooren2018_cooldown].
options.against: Active cool-downs largely fail to improve next-day performance or soreness [@VanHooren2018_cooldown], and post-exercise stretching did not meaningfully improve strength recovery or soreness [@Afonso2021_postexercise_stretch_recovery; @Herbert2011_Cochrane_stretch_DOMS].

decisions.choiceSummary: Warm up with 6 min of easy cardio, dynamic drills, 2 x 30 s of single-leg balance per leg and ramp-up sets; cool down with 2 min easy and static stretching (hamstrings every session), used for range of motion rather than recovery.
decisions.rationale:
Warming up reliably helps; the question is what it should contain. The cardio block raises body temperature, which matters most early in your biological day; making it slightly longer than usual is a practical judgement, because the extended-warm-up evidence is mixed. Dynamic drills prepare joints without the strength cost of long static holds [@Behm2016_acute_stretching], ramp-up sets rehearse the first lifts ([[rule:ramp-up]], [[tool:warmup]]), and 2 x 30 s of single-leg balance per leg, left leg first, builds balance practice into every session ([[dec:D28]]).

Stretching goes after lifting, where it costs nothing. Its aim is chronic range of motion for your toe-touch limitation ([[dec:D27]]), not recovery, for which the evidence is null. Full-range strength training improves ROM about as much as stretching [@Afonso2021_STvsStretchMeta], so the lifting and the stretching work together.
decisions.confidenceNote: Warm-up and stretching meta-analyses are reasonably consistent; the cardio duration for an early-biological-day session and the exact stretch dose are judgement.

decisions.title: Aerobic training in Phase 1: modality, dose and intensity without a heart-rate monitor
decisions.context: [[term:vo2max|VO₂max]] and endurance rank just below hypertrophy and fat loss, and you start untrained. Phase 1 has to build an aerobic base and teach you to judge effort without hurting the three lifting sessions. You have no heart-rate monitor, sit through a 16:00-01:00 desk shift and face daytime heat.

options.name: Two RPE-guided sessions a week on non-lifting days
options.summary: A steady session building from 20 to 35 min at [[term:rpe|RPE]] 3-4 (you can still talk in full sentences: the [[term:talk-test|talk test]]) and, from week 7, 6-8 x 1 min hard / 2 min easy. Any machine you like, incline treadmill walking by default. Steps: 8,000-10,000 a day, never below 7,000.
options.for: Untrained people showed no measurable hypertrophy or maximal-strength cost from added aerobic work [@Schumann2021_concurrentMA; @Petre2021_trainingStatusMA], and continuous and interval training both raise VO₂max by about 5 mL/kg/min [@Milanovic2015_HITvsCET_VO2maxMA]. The point where speech first becomes difficult sits near the [[term:ventilatory-threshold|ventilatory threshold]] [@Persinger2004_talkTest; @ReedPipe2014_talkTestReview], and RPE tracks blood lactate (r = 0.83) [@Scherr2013_RPE].
options.against: 40-70 min a week is below the WHO range of 150-300 min of moderate activity [@Bull2020_WHOguidelines] unless brisk walking within your steps fills the gap (inference).

options.name: No cardio in Phase 1
options.summary: Lift only and start aerobic work in Phase 2.
options.for: An older meta-analysis found smaller hypertrophy gains with concurrent training (ES 0.85 vs 1.23) [@Wilson2012_concurrentMA].
options.against: Newer pooled data show no such cost [@Schumann2021_concurrentMA], and unfit people gain VO₂max fastest [@Milanovic2015_HITvsCET_VO2maxMA].

options.name: Intervals only
options.summary: Two short [[term:hiit|HIIT]] sessions a week from week 1.
options.for: HIIT beat [[term:mict|moderate-intensity continuous training (MICT)]] for VO₂max by 1.39 mL/kg/min [@Strauss2026_CochraneHIIT], and [[term:zone-2|zone 2]] work has no special status [@Storoschuk2025_zone2Review].
options.against: That edge is low certainty [@Strauss2026_CochraneHIIT]; a beginner must learn pacing first, and hard sessions add fatigue in the sorest early weeks of lifting (inference).

options.name: Daily long sessions, or running from day one
options.summary: 45-60 min on most days, or running as the main mode.
options.for: A higher dose leaves fewer non-responders: 69% at one 60-min session a week, none at four or five [@MonteroLundby2017_nonresponse].
options.against: Longer and more frequent endurance work correlated with smaller strength and size gains [@Wilson2012_concurrentMA], and novices are injured about twice as often per running hour as recreational runners [@Videbaek2015_runningInjuryIncidence].

decisions.choiceSummary: Do two aerobic sessions a week on non-lifting days at RPE 3-4, building from 20 to 35 min with short intervals from week 7, on any machine (incline walking by default), and walk 8,000-10,000 steps a day (floor 7,000).
decisions.rationale:
The dose is one that builds fitness without measurable [[term:interference-effect|interference]] in beginners [@Schumann2021_concurrentMA].

Intensity is set by feel because heart-rate zones would rest on an age-predicted [[term:hrmax|HRmax]] (about 186 bpm at 31 by the Tanaka equation [@Tanaka2001_HRmax], 191 by the HUNT equation) with a standard error of about 11 bpm, so roughly ±20 bpm for an individual [@Nes2013_HUNT_HRmax]. RPE and the talk test cost nothing and work on any machine.

Steady work first, with intervals from week 7, is practical convention: you learn pacing while early lifting soreness settles. Incline walking needs no skill, has low impact and works indoors in the heat; running waits for Phase 2 ([[dec:D14]]). Steps add daily movement: mortality risk levelled off at about 8,000-10,000 a day in adults under 60 (observational) [@Paluch2022_stepsMortalityMA].
decisions.confidenceNote: The interference and VO₂max findings are moderate certainty; session lengths, the week-7 interval start and the walking default are practical convention.

decisions.title: Upper/lower split and volume for aesthetic priorities (Phase 2)
decisions.context: Phase 2 (16 weeks) starts shaping the look you want: athletic, not bulky. That look comes mostly from the lateral and rear deltoids, upper chest, back and arms. Giving those muscles 12-16 [[term:hard-sets|weekly sets]] while still training legs is hard to fit into three sessions between 13:00 and work at 16:00.

options.name: Four upper/lower sessions, priority muscles first
options.summary: Upper A, lower A, upper B, lower B. Priority muscles get 12-16 [[term:fractional-sets|fractional sets]] a week, lateral raises appear on three days, each day opens with a priority exercise, and legs get about 10-13 sets.
options.for: Hypertrophy rises with weekly volume, with diminishing returns [@Pelland2025_volume_frequency]; at equal volume, split and [[term:training-frequency|frequency]] barely matter [@Schoenfeld2019_frequency_hypertrophy; @RamosCampo2024_split_vs_fullbody]. Cues of upper-body strength explained over 70% of the variance in rated male attractiveness [@Sell2017_strengthAttractiveness], and a V-shaped torso was the main predictor in urban samples [@Swami2005_WCRcrossCultural].
options.against: A fourth gym day costs time, exercise order did not change hypertrophy overall [@Nunes2021_exerciseOrderMeta], and the perception studies are cross-sectional with preferences that varied by setting [@Swami2005_WCRcrossCultural].

options.name: Stay full-body three times a week
options.summary: Keep the Phase 1 structure and add sets.
options.for: Full-body and split routines give similar strength and hypertrophy at equal volume [@RamosCampo2024_split_vs_fullbody].
options.against: The added sets would make three sessions too long for your schedule, with the last sets done tired (inference).

options.name: Push/pull/legs, six days a week
options.summary: Each muscle twice a week over six shorter sessions.
options.for: Without volume matching, higher frequency gave a modest hypertrophy edge, explained by the extra volume it allowed [@Schoenfeld2019_frequency_hypertrophy].
options.against: With volume accounted for, frequency had a negligible, uncertain effect [@Pelland2025_volume_frequency], and six lifting days leave no day for intervals or rest (inference).

options.name: Body-part split
options.summary: Each muscle once a week over five sessions.
options.for: Weekly frequency did not change hypertrophy at equal volume [@Schoenfeld2019_frequency_hypertrophy].
options.against: Five gym days, all of a muscle's 12-16 sets in one session, and fewer weekly practice exposures for lifts you are still learning (inference).

decisions.choiceSummary: Train four upper/lower sessions a week, with 12-16 weekly sets for the lateral and rear deltoids, upper chest, back and arms (lateral raises on three days, a priority exercise first) and about 10-13 for the legs.
decisions.rationale:
Split and frequency matter little once weekly volume is matched [@Schoenfeld2019_frequency_hypertrophy; @RamosCampo2024_split_vs_fullbody], so the split is a logistics choice: four sessions hold the higher volume, end before work and leave days for intervals and run-walk ([[dec:D13]], [[dec:D14]]).

Volume is the [[term:hypertrophy|hypertrophy]] lever [@Pelland2025_volume_frequency], so extra sets go where they change your silhouette most, while legs stay at a moderate dose that suits the 'not bulky' aim (inference). The priority list rests on cross-sectional perception research and your stated preference, not on outcome trials.

A priority exercise goes first so its sets are done fresh (practical convention); doing an exercise first also favours its strength gains [@Nunes2021_exerciseOrderMeta].
decisions.confidenceNote: The split, frequency and volume findings are moderate certainty; the priority list rests on low-certainty perception studies and your preference, and set numbers are convention.

decisions.title: Interval protocol for VO2max (4 x 4) and scheduling around lifting
decisions.context: [[term:vo2max|VO₂max]] is one of your goals and a strong marker of health, but lifting has priority and time is limited. Phase 2 adds one hard session aimed squarely at VO₂max while running is still being introduced and you have no heart-rate monitor.

options.name: One 4 x 4-min session a week on a non-lifting day
options.summary: 4 x 4 min at [[term:rpe|RPE]] 8-9 with 3-min easy recoveries (3-min intervals in weeks 1-3; 6 x 2 min in the Phase 3 strength block), on a bike, rower or incline treadmill until running is established. A second weekly session is added if VO₂max stops improving.
options.for: Long intervals (2 min or more) with at least 15 min of hard work gave the largest VO₂max effects and were the only formats to beat continuous training [@Wen2019_HIITprotocolsMA]; 4 x 4 raised VO₂max 7.2% in 8 weeks in moderately trained men [@Helgerud2007_4x4RCT] and beat sprint intervals head to head in well-trained men [@Hov2022_HIITvsSIT_RCT].
options.against: Those trials used three sessions a week, and non-response falls as dose rises (69% non-responders with one 60-min session a week) [@MonteroLundby2017_nonresponse].

options.name: Steady training only
options.summary: Longer [[term:mict|moderate-intensity continuous training (MICT)]] instead of intervals.
options.for: Waist reduction did not differ from interval training [@Strauss2026_CochraneHIIT], and the sessions are more comfortable.
options.against: Smaller VO₂max gains: intervals beat continuous training by 1.2 mL/kg/min, and by 2.2 with longer intervals [@Milanovic2015_HITvsCET_VO2maxMA].

options.name: Sprint intervals (all-out 20-30 s)
options.summary: Short maximal efforts ([[term:sit|SIT]]).
options.for: Very time-efficient: about +3.6 mL/kg/min (8%), similar to continuous training [@Gist2014_SITmeta].
options.against: 4 x 4 beat sprint formats in two head-to-head trials in well-trained runners from one research group [@Hov2022_HIITvsSIT_RCT; @Helgerud2023_HIITvsSIT_femaleRCT], all-out treadmill sprinting caused 8 injuries versus none with 4 x 4 [@Helgerud2023_HIITvsSIT_femaleRCT], and the SIT comparisons carry unclear risk of bias [@Bonafiglia2021_SITvsMICTbias].

options.name: Two sessions a week, one after lifting
options.summary: Double the interval dose by adding a session to a lifting day.
options.for: More dose means fewer non-responders [@MonteroLundby2017_nonresponse], and exercise order within a session did not change VO₂max or lower-body hypertrophy [@Eddens2018_sequenceMA].
options.against: Same-session work blunted explosive strength unless the modes were 3 h or more apart [@Schumann2021_concurrentMA], and added HIIT slightly reduced lower-body strength gains (ES -0.25) [@Sabag2018_HIITconcurrentMA].

decisions.choiceSummary: Do one 4 x 4-min interval session a week at RPE 8-9 with 3-min easy recoveries, on a non-lifting day and on a bike, rower or incline treadmill until running is established, adding a second session if VO₂max stalls.
decisions.rationale:
Long intervals gave the largest VO₂max gains [@Wen2019_HIITprotocolsMA; @Helgerud2007_4x4RCT]. VO₂max gains come largely from expanded red-cell volume and [[term:stroke-volume|stroke volume]] [@Lundby2017_biologyVO2max], and several minutes near maximal heart rate load exactly that system (mechanistic reasoning); against no exercise, interval training adds about 6 mL/kg/min [@Strauss2026_CochraneHIIT].

The cardio dossier suggested two sessions a week. One was chosen because hypertrophy ranks higher and time is limited, a trade against the dose-response for non-response [@MonteroLundby2017_nonresponse], so the plan adds a second session if your field tests stall ([[rule:cardio-progression]]). A separate day protects explosive strength [@Schumann2021_concurrentMA]. The shorter opening intervals and the 6 x 2 strength-block variant are practical convention.
decisions.confidenceNote: Several RCTs and meta-analyses favour long intervals, but the 4 x 4 trials are small, mostly running-based and used three sessions a week; one session is a pragmatic dose.

decisions.title: Introducing running: run-walk and the spike rule
decisions.context: Running is the most portable aerobic exercise and the 2.4 km test needs it, but new runners are injured often and you have never run regularly. Phase 2 introduces one run a week; the question is how to dose it.

options.name: Run-walk with a session-spike cap
options.summary: A weekly run-walk starting at 8 min of running in total; no session's running more than about 10% above your longest run of the previous 30 days; treadmill in heat; comfortable cushioned shoes; [[term:pain-monitoring|pain monitoring]]; about 24 min continuous by week 15 (or 2 x 12 min with a 1-min walk if continuous feels too big a step).
options.for: In 5,200 mostly experienced adult runners, sessions 10-30% longer than the 30-day longest run carried 1.64 times the injury rate and spikes above 100% 2.28 times, while weekly load ratios showed no excess risk [@Frandsen2025_spikes]. Harder shoes raised injury risk (SHR 1.52), mainly in lighter runners [@Malisoux2020_cushioning].
options.against: The spike data are observational and the cap is untested in a trial [@Frandsen2025_spikes]; the shoe evidence overall is low certainty [@Relph2022_shoesCochrane].

options.name: Continuous running from the start
options.summary: Run without walk breaks from week 1.
options.for: Untrained men raised VO₂max 21.5% in 12 weeks of moderate continuous running, partly through weight loss [@Milanovic2015_untrainedMenRunningRCT].
options.against: Novices are injured about twice as often per running hour as recreational runners [@Videbaek2015_runningInjuryIncidence], and in one small trial in obese novices a larger starting dose trended towards more injuries [@Bertelsen2018_starttorun].

options.name: The '10% weekly rule'
options.summary: Raise weekly distance by no more than 10%.
options.for: Progression above 30% over two weeks trended towards more distance-related injuries (HR 1.59, p = 0.07) [@Nielsen2014_progression].
options.against: A graded 10%-rule programme did not reduce injuries (20.8% vs 20.3%) [@Buist2008_GRONORUN], and weekly load ratios were not linked to risk [@Frandsen2025_spikes].

options.name: No running (cycling only)
options.summary: Keep all aerobic work on the bike or rower.
options.for: No running injuries, and one meta-analysis found that running, but not cycling, reduced strength and size gains [@Wilson2012_concurrentMA].
options.against: A newer analysis found no difference between running and cycling [@Schumann2021_concurrentMA], and you would lose the most portable mode and the run test (inference).

decisions.choiceSummary: Run once a week in Phase 2 with run-walk sessions that start at 8 min of running and never exceed your longest run of the previous 30 days by more than about 10%, building to about 24 min continuous by week 15 (or 2 x 12 min with a 1-min walk if continuous feels too big a step).
decisions.rationale:
The best evidence points at single-session spikes rather than weekly progression: the 10% rule did not prevent injuries [@Buist2008_GRONORUN], while sessions well beyond the recent longest run carried more risk [@Frandsen2025_spikes]. That cohort is observational, so the cap is a precaution, not a proven intervention. A small start follows a trend in a small trial [@Bertelsen2018_starttorun] (very low certainty); walk breaks are practical convention.

Comfortable cushioned shoes are cheap insurance at your body mass [@Malisoux2020_cushioning]; choosing shoes by foot type is not supported [@Relph2022_shoesCochrane; @Nielsen2014_pronation]. The treadmill in heat and the pain rules are practical convention ([[rule:running]], [[rule:pain]], [[tool:running]]).
decisions.confidenceNote: Low to moderate: the high novice injury rate is well established, but the spike rule rests on one observational cohort, shoe evidence is low certainty, and the 8-to-24-min progression is convention.

decisions.title: Barbell lifts with safety arms vs machines only
decisions.context: You train alone, so nobody can spot or rescue a failed lift. Barbell squats, Romanian deadlifts and bench presses build strength in those movements, while machines are safer places to push hard. The question is whether barbells belong in your programme, and under what conditions.

options.name: Barbells inside a rack with safety arms, never to failure
options.summary: Barbell squat and Romanian deadlift from Phase 2; barbell bench press only in the Phase 3 strength block; [[term:safety-arms|safety arms]] always set; barbell sets stop at 2-3 [[term:rir|reps in reserve (RIR)]]; near-failure sets on machines.
options.for: Hypertrophy was similar with free weights and machines (wide confidence intervals), but strength gains are specific to the trained movement [@Haugen2023_freeVsMachineMeta; @Saeterbakken2025_taskSpecificityMeta]. Weights dropping on the lifter caused 65.5% of weight-training injuries seen in US emergency departments [@Kerr2010_weightTrainingED], the hazard safety arms address.
options.against: It needs a free rack and technique practice, no study has tested safety arms (inference), and barbells added no clear hypertrophy benefit [@Haugen2023_freeVsMachineMeta].

options.name: Machines only
options.summary: No barbell work at all.
options.for: Similar hypertrophy [@Haugen2023_freeVsMachineMeta], and machine injuries were less often fractures or dislocations (9.7% vs 23.6%) [@Kerr2010_weightTrainingED].
options.against: Barbell strength would lag, because strength gains are largely specific to the movement trained [@Saeterbakken2025_taskSpecificityMeta].

options.name: Free barbells without safeties, sets to failure
options.summary: Treat barbell lifts like machines and push sets to [[term:momentary-failure|momentary failure]].
options.for: In an exploratory meta-regression, hypertrophy increased as sets ended closer to failure [@Robinson2024_RIR_metaregression].
options.against: Reaching failure adds little over stopping close [@Refalo2023_failure_hypertrophy], barely mattered with heavy loads in one trial [@Lasevicius2022_failure_by_load] and delayed recovery by 24-48 h in another [@MoranNavarro2017_failure_recovery]; alone, a failed squat or bench can trap you (inference).

decisions.choiceSummary: Use the barbell squat and Romanian deadlift from Phase 2 and the barbell bench press only in the Phase 3 strength block, always inside a rack with safety arms and never to failure, and keep near-failure sets for machines.
decisions.rationale:
You do not need barbells for muscle [@Haugen2023_freeVsMachineMeta], but strength is largely skill in the tested movement [@Saeterbakken2025_taskSpecificityMeta], and barbell competence serves the strength block and later years.

Injury rates in weight-training sports are low, with bodybuilding at 0.24-1 per 1,000 h [@Keogh2017_weightTrainingInjury]; the specific solo risk is a load you cannot complete, and dropped weights dominate emergency-department data [@Kerr2010_weightTrainingED]. Safety arms and a 2-3 RIR ceiling remove most of that risk at little cost, since in one trial failure added almost nothing to growth with heavy loads [@Lasevicius2022_failure_by_load]; the safety benefit itself is inference. Near-failure effort moves to machines, where failing is harmless ([[dec:D07]]). The bench press comes last because a bar stuck on the chest is the most dangerous solo failure (inference).
decisions.confidenceNote: Hypertrophy equivalence and strength specificity are meta-analytic findings; the benefit of safety arms and of stopping short of failure is inference from injury-mechanism data.

A reliable training partner who can spot

decisions.title: Phase 3 block structure
decisions.context: By Phase 3 you will have trained for about 29 weeks, novice gains will be slowing, and strength, power and conditioning join the goals. You also need variety to stay engaged. The question is how to organise the 24 weeks.

options.name: Three 8-week emphasis blocks with mixed sessions
options.summary: Hypertrophy; strength and power; physique and conditioning. Blocks 1 and 2 end with a planned deload week (weeks 8 and 16), anchor exercises stay fixed within a block, and every week still trains all qualities.
options.for: In one small trial in trained men, mixing qualities within sessions beat classical blocks for fat-free mass, muscle thickness and bench 1RM (+8.6% vs +2%) [@Bartolomei2023_blockVsMixed]. Heavier loads raise [[term:1rm|1RM]] more [@Lopez2021_load_NMA], and planned, reasoned variation can aid regional growth while random rotation may blunt it [@Kassiano2022_variationSR].
options.against: No trial tests this exact design, and periodisation gives no hypertrophy advantage [@Moesgaard2022_periodization], so the blocks mainly serve focus and variety (inference).

options.name: Continue non-periodised training
options.summary: Keep the Phase 2 structure.
options.for: Periodised and non-periodised training gave similar hypertrophy at equal volume [@Moesgaard2022_periodization].
options.against: Periodised plans gave larger 1RM gains (ES 0.43; 0.31 with volume equated) [@Williams2017_periodization; @Moesgaard2022_periodization], and strength now matters to you.

options.name: Classical block periodisation
options.summary: One quality per block, with large shifts in volume and load.
options.for: It improved vertical jump more than mixed sessions (+7.2% vs +1.2%) [@Bartolomei2023_blockVsMixed].
options.against: It lost to mixed sessions for muscle and bench strength in the same trial [@Bartolomei2023_blockVsMixed].

options.name: Daily undulating periodisation only
options.summary: Rotate heavy, moderate and light days without blocks.
options.for: Undulating beat linear periodisation for 1RM in trained people [@Moesgaard2022_periodization].
options.against: No hypertrophy difference from linear models (d -0.02) [@Grgic2017_LPvsDUP_hypertrophy], and you already undulate mildly from Phase 2 (inference).

decisions.choiceSummary: Run Phase 3 as three 8-week emphasis blocks (hypertrophy; strength and power; physique and conditioning), the first two ending with a planned deload week, anchor exercises fixed within each block and all qualities still trained every week.
decisions.rationale:
With volume matched, [[term:periodisation|periodisation]] adds a little strength but no muscle [@Moesgaard2022_periodization; @Williams2017_periodization; @Grgic2017_LPvsDUP_hypertrophy], so the blocks are built for focus and variety rather than extra growth.

Training every quality each week follows the one head-to-head trial, in which mixed sessions beat classical blocks for muscle and bench strength [@Bartolomei2023_blockVsMixed]; it was a single small study in trained men. The strength-and-power block uses heavier loads because they raise 1RM more, while growth is similar across loads [@Lopez2021_load_NMA]. Anchors stay fixed so progress is trackable and variation stays systematic [@Kassiano2022_variationSR]. The lighter weeks (weeks 8 and 16) are planned [[term:deload|deloads]] (practical convention; [[rule:deload]]).
decisions.confidenceNote: Low to moderate: the periodisation meta-analyses agree, but the block-versus-mixed comparison is one small trial in trained men, and block length and order are practical choices.

decisions.title: Power, agility, balance and coordination: how to train them
decisions.context: Power, agility, balance and coordination are your lowest priorities, but they shape how athletic you move, and your left leg balances worse than your right (20 vs 30 s eyes open, 10 vs 15 s eyes closed). The aim is to train them without taking time from the main goals.

options.name: Small doses inside existing sessions
options.summary: Single-leg balance in every warm-up (left first) plus [[term:unilateral|unilateral]] lifts; [[term:plyometrics|plyometrics]] in Phase 3 lower-body warm-ups (about 36 contacts, well under 250 a week); brief agility drills in Block 3; coordination through a skill you enjoy, such as dance or a martial art.
options.for: Plyometrics improve countermovement jump height (+8.7%) [@Markovic2007_vertjump], [[term:rsi|reactive strength]] (ES 0.54) [@RamirezCampillo2023_RSI] and balance (ES 0.46) [@Ramachandran2021_plyobalance], with larger stiffness gains below 250 jumps a week [@Moran2023_stiffness]. Dance improved musculoskeletal function more than other exercise [@FongYan2018_danceMA].
options.against: The balance dose is far below the 11-15 min three times a week that worked best [@Lesinski2015_balanceDR], and balance gains barely transfer beyond the practised task [@Kummel2016_specificity].

options.name: Dedicated balance sessions
options.summary: 11-15 min, three times a week, for 11-12 weeks.
options.for: The most effective dose in a dose-response meta-analysis [@Lesinski2015_balanceDR]; [[term:proprioception|proprioceptive]] training reduced sports injuries (RR 0.55) [@Lauersen2014_injury_prevention].
options.against: Gains stay specific to the trained task [@Kummel2016_specificity], and plyometrics improved balance about as much as balance training [@Ramachandran2021_plyobalance].

options.name: Agility-ladder programmes
options.summary: Regular ladder and cone footwork sessions.
options.for: Many training forms improve change-of-direction ability [@NygaardFalch2019_COD].
options.against: No form is superior and the skill is task-specific [@NygaardFalch2019_COD]; without a sport, ladder practice mostly improves ladder practice (inference).

options.name: Ignore these goals
options.summary: Lift and do cardio only.
options.for: Strength training alone strongly reduced sports injuries (RR 0.34) [@Lauersen2018_strength].
options.against: Your balance asymmetry would go unaddressed, and plyometrics improved reactive strength beyond what active controls achieved [@RamirezCampillo2023_RSI].

decisions.choiceSummary: Train these qualities in small doses inside existing sessions: single-leg balance in every warm-up (left side first), unilateral lifts, low-volume plyometrics in Phase 3 warm-ups, brief agility drills in Block 3, and coordination through a skill you enjoy.
decisions.rationale:
These qualities are task-specific: balance training improves the practised task but not others [@Kummel2016_specificity], and change-of-direction ability follows training that resembles the target task [@NygaardFalch2019_COD]. Ranked last, they get small doses placed where they cost little time.

Plyometrics probably give the broadest return per minute (inference) [@Markovic2007_vertjump; @Ramachandran2021_plyobalance]; the low contact count is also a joint-load precaution, because most trials did not report injuries [@RamirezCampillo2023_RSI] (inference). Strength training remains the main injury-prevention tool [@Lauersen2018_strength]. For coordination, dance improved body composition and musculoskeletal function [@FongYan2018_danceMA] and combat sports improved long jump and flexibility in students [@HernandezMartinez2025_combatsports]; which you choose should follow enjoyment (inference). Expect only modest change in the single-leg test ([[dec:D28]]).
decisions.confidenceNote: Low to moderate: single effects (plyometrics on jumping, balance training on the trained task) are meta-analytic, but transfer evidence is weak and the embedded doses are smaller than those studied.

decisions.title: Long-term continuation and maintenance doses
decisions.context: After the first year you need a way to keep progressing and a fallback for busy periods, travel or illness. Knowing the smallest dose that keeps muscle, strength and [[term:vo2max|VO₂max]] lets you protect your gains without all-or-nothing thinking.

options.name: Repeating 12-week cycles with a defined maintenance dose
options.summary: 12-week cycles with a chosen emphasis; maintenance at about 6-8 [[term:hard-sets|hard sets]] per muscle a week at usual effort plus one interval and one steady session; Maintenance mode (about one-third of usual volume, main lifts at 2-3 RIR) for busy periods. The two doses answer different questions: 6-8 sets a week holds one muscle you are happy with while the rest of the programme continues indefinitely; Maintenance mode is a short-term holding pattern for the whole body when time is scarce.
options.for: In one small trial in young adults, one-third (even one-ninth) of the training dose preserved hypertrophy for 32 weeks [@Bickel2011_maintenanceDose], and endurance held with two sessions a week when intensity was kept [@Spiering2021_minimalDose].
options.against: Maintenance data are few and small, and 6-8 sets exceeds the reported minimum for younger people (one set per exercise once a week), so it costs some extra time [@Spiering2021_minimalDose].

options.name: Open-ended routine without cycles
options.summary: Keep training the same way indefinitely.
options.for: In one small trial, six months of continuous training gave gains similar to training with planned breaks [@Ogasawara2013_periodicVsContinuous].
options.against: The continuous group's rate of gain slowed after six weeks [@Ogasawara2013_periodicVsContinuous], and there are no planned reassessments or variety (inference).

options.name: Stop completely when busy
options.summary: Pause training and restart later.
options.for: Gains during retraining after a 3-week break were rapid [@Ogasawara2013_periodicVsContinuous].
options.against: Strength and power fall with time off, more with longer breaks [@Bosquet2013_detrainingMeta], and lean-mass gains were no longer present after detraining [@Zhang2026_detrainingBodyComp].

decisions.choiceSummary: After the first year, train in repeating 12-week cycles with a chosen emphasis, hold gains with about 6-8 hard sets per muscle a week plus one interval and one steady session when progress is not the aim, and switch to Maintenance mode (main lifts at 2-3 RIR) rather than stopping in busy periods.
decisions.rationale:
Adaptations are cheaper to keep than to build. In one small trial, one-third of the original dose kept hypertrophy in young adults [@Bickel2011_maintenanceDose], and strength and size can be held with very low volume if loads stay heavy [@Spiering2021_minimalDose]. Maintenance mode sits near the roughly 4 weekly sets per muscle proposed as a time-efficient minimum [@Iversen2021_time_efficient]; the 6-8-set dose leaves a margin because the data are sparse (inference).

Stopping is the worst option: [[term:detraining|detraining]] costs strength [@Bosquet2013_detrainingMeta] and lean mass [@Zhang2026_detrainingBodyComp]. Short breaks are probably not disasters, since regain was quick in one small trial [@Ogasawara2013_periodicVsContinuous] ([[rule:breaks]]). The 12-week cycle gives regular reassessment and planned variety (practical convention).
decisions.confidenceNote: Maintenance and detraining data come from a few small trials, one meta-analysis and narrative reviews, mostly in previously untrained people; cycle length and set numbers are practical choices.
