decisions.title: Protein target and distribution
decisions.context: Protein supplies the amino acids for [[term:mps|muscle protein synthesis (MPS)]] while you pursue [[term:recomposition|body recomposition]] ([[dec:D04]]). You eat four meals across a 12:00-04:00 waking day, probably with legumes supplying part of the protein.

options.name: About 1.8 g/kg a day (range 1.6-2.2) over four meals
options.summary: About 140 g a day at 77 kg (floor about 125 g), 2.0-2.4 g/kg (about 170 g) in any dedicated fat-loss block, and about 30-45 g (at least about 0.4 g/kg) per meal, the last a protein-rich meal before sleep.
options.for: Added protein during training raised [[term:ffm|fat-free mass]] by 0.30 kg, with no further gain above about 1.62 g/kg/day [@Morton2018_proteinRT]; under 65, the benefit appeared only at 1.6 g/kg/day or more [@Nunes2022_proteinLBM]. In a deficit, intake above the recommended dietary allowance (RDA) cut lean-mass loss by 0.36 kg [@Hudson2020_aboveRDA].
options.against: The breakpoint comes from comparisons between trials rather than within them [@Morton2018_proteinRT], so intake above 1.6 g/kg is insurance that costs food and money (inference).

options.name: The RDA (0.8 g/kg a day)
options.summary: About 62 g a day.
options.for: It is the cheapest option, and without training or dieting, extra protein did not change lean mass [@Hudson2020_aboveRDA].
options.against: With resistance training, intake above the RDA added 0.77 kg of lean mass [@Hudson2020_aboveRDA].

options.name: About 1.2 g/kg a day
options.summary: About 90-95 g a day.
options.for: Lean mass rose most steeply below about 1.3 g/kg/day (+0.39 kg per extra 0.1 g/kg) [@Tagawa2021_doseLBM], and strength gains levelled off at about 1.5 g/kg/day [@Tagawa2022_doseStrength].
options.against: Under 65, the lean-mass benefit was significant only at 1.6 g/kg/day or more [@Nunes2022_proteinLBM], and lean mass kept rising, more slowly, above 1.3 g/kg/day [@Tagawa2021_doseLBM].

options.name: 3 g/kg a day or more
options.summary: About 230 g a day or more.
options.for: Lean, trained people in larger deficits may need 2.3-3.1 g/kg of fat-free mass [@Helms2014_deficit; @Jager2017_ISSNprotein], and diets of 1.5 g/kg/day or more did not change kidney function in healthy adults over the trials' durations [@Devries2018_kidney].
options.against: Muscle gain did not rise above about 1.6 g/kg/day [@Morton2018_proteinRT]; 3.1 g/kg of fat-free mass is only about 2.5 g/kg of your body mass; and such intakes are costly, filling and crowd out carbohydrate (inference).

decisions.choiceSummary: Eat about 1.8 g of protein per kg of body mass a day (about 140 g; range 1.6-2.2, floor about 125 g) and 2.0-2.4 g/kg in any dedicated fat-loss block, spread as about 30-45 g (at least about 0.4 g/kg) over your four meals with a protein-rich meal before sleep.
decisions.rationale:
Extra protein helps only alongside training or a deficit [@Hudson2020_aboveRDA], and its benefit flattens near 1.6 g/kg/day [@Morton2018_proteinRT] without stopping dead [@Tagawa2021_doseLBM]. Aiming about 0.2 g/kg higher covers that uncertainty, logging error and the lower digestibility of legume protein [@Kashyap2019_legumeTID] (inference). A deficit raises the need, more so as you get leaner [@Helms2014_deficit], hence the higher fat-loss band ([[rule:phase-nutrition]]).

Per meal, in acute tracer studies, MPS after leg exercise was near-maximal at about 20 g, with the surplus oxidised [@Witard2014_wheyDose], but 40 g beat 20 g by about 20% after whole-body training [@Macnaughton2016_20v40], so there is no hard ceiling. Four meals of about 0.4 g/kg [@SchoenfeldAragon2018_perMeal] are a reliable route to the total rather than a proven lever, since meal frequency did not change body composition [@Schoenfeld2015_mealFreq]. Pre-sleep protein improved strength and quadriceps size over 12 weeks, though total intake also differed [@Snijders2015_presleep]; meal times are in [[dec:D20]].
decisions.confidenceNote: The dose findings come from several moderate-certainty meta-analyses; the fat-loss band, per-meal amounts and pre-sleep timing rest on small trials, consensus and inference.

decisions.title: Meal timing around a 13:00 session and a late schedule
decisions.context: You wake at 12:00, train at about 13:00, work 16:00-01:00 and sleep at 04:00, so your first meal sits close to training and your last close to bed. Meal times decide whether you train after a fast of about 10 h and whether late eating disturbs your sleep.

options.name: Four meals anchored to training, work and sleep
options.summary: Meal 1 at about 12:15, 45 min before training: easy to digest, 30-40 g protein and 40-70 g carbohydrate, little fat or fibre. Meal 2 at about 14:45 after training; meal 3 at the work break (19:30-20:00); meal 4 eaten between about 01:15 and 02:00 (finished by about 02:00, so about 2 h before the 04:00 bedtime), protein-rich.
options.for: Carbohydrate before lifting helped in 6 of 19 acute studies, mainly against fasted controls [@Henselmans2022_carbRT], your state after the night, and the pre-exercise meal sets how urgent post-exercise protein is [@Kerksick2017_ISSNtiming].
options.against: Fed and fasted training did not differ significantly for muscle or strength in four small trials [@Vieira2025_fastedRT], and in a cross-sectional survey, eating within 3 h of bed was linked to more night waking (odds ratio 1.61) [@Chung2020_mealProximitySleep].

options.name: Fasted training
options.summary: Water only before the session; first meal afterwards.
options.for: Four small trials found no significant difference in [[term:ffm|fat-free mass]], [[term:hypertrophy|hypertrophy]] or strength, and more fat loss with fasted training ([[term:smd|SMD]] -1.00) [@Vieira2025_fastedRT].
options.against: The certainty is very low and the intervals wide [@Vieira2025_fastedRT], carbohydrate helped mainly against fasted controls [@Henselmans2022_carbRT], and you would go about 13 h without food by meal 2 (inference).

options.name: Three larger meals
options.summary: About 45-55 g protein at each meal.
options.for: Meal frequency did not change body composition with energy and protein matched [@Schoenfeld2015_mealFreq], and 100 g of protein gave a longer anabolic response than 25 g [@Trommelen2023_100g].
options.against: Consensus favours 20-40 g every 3-4 h [@Kerksick2017_ISSNtiming], and on your day one of the pre-training, post-training or post-work meals would go (inference).

options.name: Time-restricted eating
options.summary: All food within an 8-10-h window, for example 12:00-20:00.
options.for: In resistance-trained people it cut fat mass slightly (-1.25 kg) without a significant change in fat-free mass [@Ali2026_TRE_RT].
options.against: The fat-free-mass interval was wide (-0.80 to +1.34 kg) [@Ali2026_TRE_RT], and an 8-h window on your day drops either the post-work meal (about 16 h without food) or the meals around training (inference).

decisions.choiceSummary: Eat a light protein-and-carbohydrate meal at about 12:15, 45 min before training, the main meal at about 14:45 after it, a meal at the work break (about 19:30-20:00) and a protein-rich meal at about 01:15-02:00 that ends at least about 2 h before your 04:00 bedtime.
decisions.rationale:
Timing is secondary to the daily total: once total protein was accounted for, protein around the session did not change hypertrophy or strength [@Schoenfeld2013_timing]. The schedule serves the target in [[dec:D19]] and fits three features of your day.

Meal 1 ends a fast of about 10 h. Liver glycogen falls overnight while muscle glycogen is largely kept (established physiology), so the benefit is probably small, but it avoids the fasted state in which carbohydrate helped [@Henselmans2022_carbRT]. Keeping it light is practical convention; if early eating makes you nauseous, train fasted, except before 4 x 4 intervals, and eat within an hour afterwards.

Meal 2 refuels you before work, as post-exercise protein reliably raises [[term:mps|muscle protein synthesis (MPS)]] [@Kerksick2017_ISSNtiming].

Meal 4 doubles as pre-sleep protein, though a timing benefit beyond total intake is unproven [@Snijders2015_presleep; @Reis2020_presleepProteinSR]. Links between late eating and night waking weakened as the gap widened from 1 h to 2-3 h [@Iao2021_bedtimeEatingATUS]; a 3-h rule would push the meal into your shift, so about 2 h is the compromise (inference; [[plan:sleep]]).
decisions.confidenceNote: Low to moderate: total protein outweighing timing is moderate certainty, but fed versus fasted training rests on four very-low-certainty trials, the sleep gap on cross-sectional data, and the clock times are convention.
profileData: Wakes 12:00 and trains 13:00, after a fast of about 10 h
About 140 g protein a day over four meals (D19)

Hevy logs showing equal performance fed and fasted over 4-6 sessions
More night waking after late meals in your sleep diary (move meal 4 earlier or shrink it)

decisions.title: Supplement stack: keep, remove, add
decisions.context: Your stack is creatine, vitamin D3, vitamin K2, folic acid, vitamin B12, magnesium glycinate, omega-3 and L-theanine, plus about 100 mg of caffeine before training. Each costs money, several have upper intake limits, and supplements sold in India have documented label and contamination problems [@Philips2024_CitizensProteinProject]. Which items earn a place for a novice training for [[term:hypertrophy|hypertrophy]] and fat loss who wakes at 12:00 and sleeps at 04:00?

options.name: Evidence-graded stack
options.summary: Keep creatine, D3 and B12; make caffeine, magnesium, omega-3, L-theanine and whey optional; drop K2 and folic acid; add nothing else.
options.for: Creatine adds lean mass (+1.14 kg, 95% CI 0.69 to 1.59, partly intracellular water) and strength (Hedges g about 0.55) beyond training alone [@Desai2024_creatineBodyComp; @Wang2026_creatineThreeLevelMA]. In pooled Indian surveys, vitamin D deficiency affected about 67% of adults [@Siddiqee2021_SouthAsiaVitDPrevalence] and B12 deficiency about 53% across age groups [@Venkatesh2021_IndiaMicronutrientDeficiency], so low doses are cheap insurance.
options.against: 1,000 IU/day of D3 exceeds the dietary reference intake, which the Endocrine Society conditionally suggests healthy adults under 75 avoid for disease prevention [@Demay2024_EndoSocVitDGuideline].

options.name: Keep everything
options.summary: Continue every item as now.
options.for: No change to routine; most items are low risk at modest doses.
options.against: Functional vitamin K insufficiency clusters in children and adults over 40 [@Theuwissen2014_vitKStatusHealthy]; omega-3 did not add muscle mass with training, though it improved strength in four small trials [@Uchida2024_omega3RT_MA]; magnesium's sleep data are low certainty and from older adults with insomnia [@Mah2021_magnesiumInsomniaMA]; theanine's effects are small and uncertain [@Payne2025_theanineMA]. Unneeded folic acid can mask B12 deficiency (mechanism).

options.name: Creatine only
options.summary: Stop everything except creatine and ordinary coffee.
options.for: Spends only on the item with outcome evidence for muscle and strength [@Desai2024_creatineBodyComp].
options.against: Drops cheap cover against vitamin D and B12 deficiency, both common in India; your indoor, largely nocturnal day limits sun exposure (inference).

options.name: Test first
options.summary: Blood tests for vitamin D and B12 before deciding.
options.for: Individualises the doses.
options.against: Routine 25(OH)D testing is advised against in healthy adults [@Demay2024_EndoSocVitDGuideline], and the chosen doses are well below upper limits, so safe without a test (inference).

decisions.choiceSummary: Keep creatine (5 g/day), vitamin D3 (1,000 IU/day) and vitamin B12; make caffeine, magnesium, omega-3, L-theanine and whey optional; stop vitamin K2 and folic acid; and add nothing else.
decisions.rationale:
The verdicts follow the supplements dossier; the daily schedule is on [[plan:supplements]].

| Item | Verdict | Dose and timing |
|---|---|---|
| Creatine monohydrate | Keep | 5 g/day with a meal, every day |
| Vitamin D3 | Keep | 1,000 IU/day with a fat-containing meal; never over 4,000 IU/day unprescribed |
| Vitamin B12 | Keep | 250-500 µg/day |
| Caffeine | Optional | 150-200 mg at 12:00 on training days; none after 19:00 |
| Magnesium glycinate | Optional | 4-week trial, 100-200 mg elemental with meal 4; total supplemental magnesium no more than 350 mg/day |
| Omega-3 | Optional | 250-500 mg/day EPA+DHA only if you eat fewer than 2 oily-fish meals a week; never above 1 g/day |
| L-theanine | Optional | 100-200 mg with the 12:00 caffeine, if you value it |
| Whey | Optional (food) | Only to close a protein gap ([[dec:D19]]) |
| K2, folic acid | Remove | Unless a doctor prescribed them |
| Beta-alanine, nitrate, citrulline, HMB | Do not add | None |
| Ashwagandha | Avoid | Including in blends |
| Melatonin | Not routinely | Fix the sleep set-up first ([[dec:D22]]) |

**Creatine** raises muscle [[term:phosphocreatine|phosphocreatine]], which regenerates ATP during hard sets; loading and daily dose did not change the effect [@Wang2026_creatineThreeLevelMA]. Serum creatinine rises by about 0.13 mg/dL with no significant change in eGFR (8 trials, wide interval) [@Tsiaras2026_creatineKidneyMA], and in one small 12-week trial 5 g/day left DHT and hair unchanged [@Lak2025_creatineHairRCT].

**Caffeine** blocks [[term:adenosine|adenosine]] receptors. Your 1.3 mg/kg is below the minimum effective dose of about 2 mg/kg [@Guest2021_ISSNcaffeine]. About 217 mg needs 13.2 h before bed and 107 mg 8.8 h [@Gardiner2023_caffeineSleepMA]: roughly 14:45 and 19:10 for a 04:00 bedtime.

**Ashwagandha** offers an uncertain benefit (prediction interval -0.40 to 1.33) [@Li2026_ashwagandhaPerformanceMA] against documented cholestatic liver injury in Indian patients, including deaths in people with existing liver disease [@Philips2023_ashwagandhaHILI_India]. **HMB** had no significant effect on fat-free mass or strength in young adults [@Jakubowski2020_HMByoungMA]. If you buy whey, choose a mainstream sports whey: these were mostly label-accurate, unlike pharmacy protein powders [@Philips2025_CitizensProteinProject2].
decisions.confidenceNote: High for keeping creatine and dropping folic acid; moderate for the D3 and B12 doses, which rest on population prevalence rather than your own status; low for the optional items. Your products' actual doses are unknown, so the upper-limit checks are provisional.

decisions.title: Sleep schedule: keep 04:00-12:00 or shift it
decisions.context: Your shift ends at 01:00, you sleep about 04:00-12:00 and you train at 13:00. Sleep affects [[term:mps|muscle protein synthesis (MPS)]], training performance and how much of the weight lost in a deficit is fat. Should the late window stay, move earlier, or flex on days off?

options.name: Fixed 04:00-12:00 every day
options.summary: The same 8-h window every day, at least 7 h asleep; a dark, quiet, cool room; bright light after waking, dim light after work; a caffeine cut-off.
options.for: Adults are advised to sleep at least 7 h regularly [@Watson2015_sleepDurationConsensus]. In 60,977 adults, more regular sleep timing went with 20-48% lower mortality, and regularity predicted mortality better than duration did [@Windred2024_sleepRegularityMortality]. A late but fixed schedule has almost no [[term:social-jetlag|social jetlag]] (inference).
options.against: Those data are observational and from older adults (mean age 63) [@Windred2024_sleepRegularityMortality], and a later modelled [[term:circadian-rhythm|circadian]] phase was also associated with higher mortality (aHR 1.13-1.20) [@Windred2024_lightExposureMortality].

options.name: Shift the window earlier
options.summary: Move sleep towards 03:00-11:00 or earlier.
options.for: In one small trial in night owls, fixed earlier sleep and wake times, morning light and fixed meal and caffeine times advanced sleep by about 2 h without shortening it and improved mood and morning grip strength [@FacerChilds2019_nightOwlPhaseAdvance].
options.against: Your work ends at 01:00, so an earlier bedtime would probably cut sleep (inference); no trial has tested this in late, non-shift workers.

options.name: Flexible on days off
options.summary: Fixed on workdays, sleep whenever suits on days off.
options.for: Social convenience.
options.against: That is social jetlag, linked in mostly cross-sectional data to slightly higher BMI (+0.49 kg/m²) and waist (+1.11 cm), though not to diabetes [@Bouman2022_socialJetlagMetabolicMA; @Arab2023_socialJetlagObesityMA]; irregular timing is also the pattern tied to higher mortality [@Windred2024_sleepRegularityMortality].

decisions.choiceSummary: Keep a fixed 04:00-12:00 sleep window (±30 min) every day, including days off, with 8 h in bed in a dark, quiet, cool room, bright light after waking, dim light after work and a caffeine cut-off.
decisions.rationale:
Your schedule is late but stable, and the evidence that matters is about duration and regularity, not clock time.

**Why protect it.** In a small crossover trial, one night without sleep cut next-day MPS by 18% [@Lamon2021_sleepDeprivationMPS]; 6 h or less reduced exercise performance by about 7.6% [@Craven2022_sleepLossPerformanceMA]; in a 14-day deficit in 10 overweight adults, 5.5 h rather than 8.5 h of sleep opportunity cut fat loss from 1.4 to 0.6 kg and raised fat-free mass loss from 1.5 to 2.4 kg [@Nedeltcheva2010_sleepCaloricRestriction]. These are harsher than your 7-8 h; the aim is to keep what you have, especially in fat-loss blocks.

**The bedroom.** Sunrise falls inside your sleep. Consensus sets 1 lux or less at the eye during sleep [@Brown2022_lightRecommendations], and one night of sleep with 100 lux of room light raised heart rate and next-morning insulin resistance [@Mason2022_lightDuringSleep]: use blackout curtains or an eye mask. Masks and earplugs improved subjective sleep, mainly in ICU studies [@Locihova2017_earplugsEyeMask], and heat increases wakefulness [@OkamotoMizuno2012_thermalEnvironment], so cool the room.

**Light and caffeine.** Light sets the clock through [[term:melanopsin|melanopsin]] cells in the retina: get daylight within 1-2 h of waking and keep light dim from 01:00 (consensus thresholds mapped onto your day, which is inference) [@Brown2022_lightRecommendations]. Caffeine cut-offs follow sleep data [@Gardiner2023_caffeineSleepMA] and are set in [[dec:D21]]. Training an hour after waking leaves some [[term:sleep-inertia|sleep inertia]], one reason the warm-up is longer ([[dec:D10]]). If insomnia persists, CBT for insomnia is the recommended first treatment [@Qaseem2016_ACPinsomniaGuideline].
decisions.confidenceNote: Duration and bedroom advice rest on consensus and laboratory studies; the regularity case is one large cohort (association, not proof of cause); applying light thresholds to a 04:00 bedtime is inference.

decisions.title: Body-composition monitoring: tape and weight trends vs BIA outputs
decisions.context: You own a foot-to-foot [[term:bia|bioelectrical impedance (BIA)]] scale that reports body fat, muscle, water, visceral fat and more. During [[term:recomposition|recomposition]] ([[dec:D04]]) scale weight may barely move while fat falls and muscle rises, so you need measures that show slow change without being swamped by noise. Which numbers should drive decisions?

options.name: Weight trend, tape and photos
options.summary: Daily morning weight as a 7-day average and multi-week trend; navel waist weekly; girths and photos every 4 weeks; a [[term:navy-method|Navy-equation]] estimate as a secondary trend; the BIA scale used only for weight.
options.for: Self-weighing added -1.7 kg (95% CI -2.6 to -0.8) within structured programmes [@Madigan2015_selfweighingMA] and was not linked overall to worse mood or disordered eating, though it had a small negative association with self-esteem [@Benn2016_selfweighingpsych]. [[term:whtr|Waist-to-height ratio]] discriminated cardiometabolic risk better than BMI [@Ashwell2012_WHtR].
options.against: No source reviewed quantified the reliability of self-measured waist; photos judged by eye are unvalidated (the only photo study tested an AI algorithm on standardised smartphone images) [@Nana2022_footBIAvsDXA]; and circumference equations underestimated DXA body fat by about 4-6 percentage points in soldiers [@McClung2025_CBEvsDXA].

options.name: Use the BIA outputs
options.summary: Decide on the scale's body-fat, muscle and visceral-fat figures.
options.for: Highly repeatable: precision error 0-0.5% body fat across 15 devices [@Siedler2022_15BIAdevices].
options.against: Individual error was 3.1-7.5% body fat, and 1.7-2.6% even for change over 12-16 weeks, probably more than a novice changes in a few months (inference) [@Siedler2022_15BIAdevices]; food, fluid and timing distort readings [@Kerr2017_foodfluid; @Tinsley2021_trackingchange]; your model has no published validation.

options.name: Periodic DXA scans
options.summary: A [[term:dxa|DXA]] scan at baseline and at each phase end.
options.for: Tracked change more robustly when pre-test standardisation slipped [@Tinsley2021_trackingchange].
options.against: Has its own error, cost and access in India were not assessed, and it gives no weekly signal (inference).

options.name: Weekly weighing
options.summary: One weigh-in a week instead of daily.
options.for: Daily and weekly weighing instructions gave similar weight loss [@Madigan2015_selfweighingMA], with less burden.
options.against: Weight cycles by about 0.3% within each week, about 0.23 kg for you [@Maher2023_weightfluctuation]; four readings a month cannot separate that from a 0 to -0.25 kg/week target.

decisions.choiceSummary: Track daily morning weight as a 7-day average and multi-week trend, navel waist weekly, girths and photos every 4 weeks, and a Navy-equation body-fat estimate as a secondary trend, using the BIA scale for weight only.
decisions.rationale:
Use measures whose error is smaller than the change you are looking for, and act on trends, never on single readings.

**Why not the BIA numbers.** The scale measures only weight and the [[term:impedance|impedance]] of a current path up one leg and down the other; fat, muscle, water and visceral fat come from proprietary equations [@Nunez1997_legtolegBIA] that hold only in the population they were built in and at normal hydration [@Kyle2004_BIAprinciples]. [[term:ffm|Fat-free mass]] is inferred from water through a fixed hydration constant of about 0.73 [@Wang1999_hydrationConstant], so starting creatine or eating a salty meal reads as tissue change.

**How to measure.** Weigh after waking and voiding, before food, caffeine or training, and change intake only on 2-4-week trends ([[rule:energy-adjustment]]). Measure waist at the navel, the site the Navy equation uses: site barely changes risk associations but shifts your value by 5 cm (86 vs 81 cm) [@Ross2008_waistprotocol], so never mix sites. Your ratio is 0.475, under 0.5, but your waist exceeds the 78 cm first action level proposed for Indian men in one study [@Misra2006_IndianWaist], though not the 90 cm consensus threshold. Body fat is shown as a range (about 17-22% across equations; working estimate about 20%, plausible 17-24%) because circumference equations underestimated DXA by about 4-6 percentage points on average [@McClung2025_CBEvsDXA] and each also carries individual error; its value lies in the trend. Photos stay a private record, never a number (practical convention). [[tool:bodycomp]] and [[tool:checkin]] do the arithmetic.
decisions.confidenceNote: High that single BIA readings are unreliable for an individual; moderate for the overall system, which no study has tested as a package.

decisions.title: Daily steps and breaking up sitting
decisions.context: Your desk shift runs 16:00-01:00, so most of your waking day after training is spent seated. Walking adds to energy expenditure through [[term:neat|non-exercise activity thermogenesis (NEAT)]], which matters for fat loss, and daily steps are among the best-studied markers of long-term health. What target should you set, and should sitting be broken up?

options.name: 7,000 floor, 8,000-10,000 target, walking breaks
options.summary: At least 7,000 steps daily, aiming for 8,000-10,000, raised gradually from your measured baseline; a 2-5 min walk every 30-60 min of the shift.
options.for: Versus 2,000 steps/day, 7,000 was associated with 47% lower all-cause mortality (HR 0.53, 95% CI 0.46-0.60), with curves flattening around 5,000-7,000 [@Ding2025_stepsHealthDoseResponse]; in adults under 60, risk fell until about 8,000-10,000 and then plateaued [@Paluch2022_stepsMortalityMA].
options.against: These are cohort associations, so the benefit of adding steps is inferred, and the break interval is practical convention with no catalogued trial behind it.

options.name: 10,000 steps from day one
options.summary: A fixed 10,000-step target from the first week.
options.for: No clear upper limit was seen within the observed range: each extra 1,000 steps/day went with 15% lower mortality (HR 0.85) [@Banach2023_stepsMortalityMA].
options.against: Most of the association is captured by 7,000-10,000 [@Ding2025_stepsHealthDoseResponse; @Paluch2022_stepsMortalityMA]; a sudden jump adds time and lower-leg load on top of five weekly sessions (inference).

options.name: Structured exercise only
options.summary: No step target; rely on lifting and cardio sessions.
options.for: WHO advises 150-300 min/week of moderate activity plus strength work on 2 or more days [@Bull2020_WHOguidelines], which your sessions only partly supply (about 40-70 aerobic minutes a week in Phase 1; [[dec:D11]]).
options.against: Sitting over 8 h/day carried no excess risk only in the most active quarter of people, at roughly 60-75 min/day of moderate activity; with low activity it went with up to 59% higher mortality (HR 1.59) [@Ekelund2016_sittingActivityMortality]. Your sessions fall well short of 60-75 min/day.

decisions.choiceSummary: Walk at least 7,000 steps every day with a target of 8,000-10,000, built up gradually, and take a short walking break every 30-60 minutes of the desk shift.
decisions.rationale:
Steps are cheap, low-fatigue activity that fits around lifting and your shift.

**Why these numbers.** The dose-response curves are steep at low counts and flatten later: risk reduction was detectable from about 2,500 steps/day, and the largest estimated benefit for mortality was at about 8,800 [@Stens2023_stepsDoseResponseMA]. A 7,000 floor keeps most of the association on busy days, and 8,000-10,000 covers the plateau for your age [@Paluch2022_stepsMortalityMA]. That adding steps causes the benefit is inference.

**Why break up sitting.** Your shift makes long [[term:sedentary-time|sedentary time]] unavoidable, and in over a million adults the excess risk of long sitting was concentrated in people who were also inactive [@Ekelund2016_sittingActivityMortality]. A short walk every 30-60 min adds steps during work hours (practical convention; no catalogued trial tests the interval).

**Why gradually.** Raise the daily average by about 1,000 steps a week from your first-week baseline (practical convention). Steps also support fat loss by raising NEAT, by an amount that varies between people; the energy check in [[tool:energy]] uses your logged average. A tracker modestly raises step counts (SMD 0.24) [@Brickwood2019_trackersMA], but a phone is enough ([[dec:D25]]).
decisions.confidenceNote: Consistent across several large meta-analyses, but all observational; the break interval and the ramp rate are practical convention.

decisions.title: Whether to buy a wearable, and what it is good for
decisions.context: Your cardio is paced by the [[term:talk-test|talk test]] and [[term:rpe|rating of perceived exertion (RPE)]] ([[dec:D11]]), your phone can count steps, and you were considering a screenless wrist band (Google Fitbit Air). A wearable adds step, heart-rate and sleep data, but each output has a different accuracy, and acting on the wrong one, such as a calorie figure, misleads diet decisions.

options.name: Optional; use only the accurate outputs
options.summary: No purchase needed. If you buy one, use steps, resting heart rate and sleep timing; use a chest strap for interval heart rate; ignore calories and sleep stages.
options.for: Major brands counted steps accurately in the laboratory [@Fuller2020_wearablesSR]; wrist optical heart rate is reasonable at rest, with errors about 30% larger during activity [@Bent2020_PPGinaccuracy]; sleep-staging Fitbits did not differ significantly from polysomnography for total sleep time [@Haghayegh2019_FitbitSleep].
options.against: No independent validation of the Fitbit Air was found, and it gates advanced features behind a subscription [@GoogleHelp2026_FitbitAir].

options.name: Buy a tracker and act on everything
options.summary: Use its calories, sleep stages and heart-rate zones to steer diet and training.
options.for: Tracker-based interventions raised daily steps (SMD 0.24, 95% CI 0.16-0.33) [@Brickwood2019_trackersMA].
options.against: No brand estimated energy expenditure accurately [@Fuller2020_wearablesSR]; consumer trackers detect wake poorly (specificity 0.18-0.54) and give inconsistent stages [@Chinoy2021_consumerSleepTrackers].

options.name: Chest strap only
options.summary: A Bluetooth strap paired with your phone for exercise heart rate.
options.for: Agreed almost perfectly with ECG (rc 0.996), while wrist devices ranged 0.67-0.92 [@Gillinov2017_HRmonitors].
options.against: No steps or sleep data, and your intervals are prescribed by RPE anyway ([[dec:D13]]).

options.name: Phone only
options.summary: Count steps with the phone; no device.
options.for: Free and already with you.
options.against: The only phone step study in the catalogue was very low quality, with limits of agreement of -573 to +377 steps over a 1,500-step walk [@Caputo2021_smartphoneSteps].

decisions.choiceSummary: A wearable is not needed; if you buy one, use it for step and resting-heart-rate trends and sleep timing, add a chest strap if you want accurate interval heart rate, and ignore its calorie and sleep-stage estimates.
decisions.rationale:
Nothing in the programme depends on a device: effort is set by RPE and the talk test, resting heart rate can be counted by hand ([[ex:test-rhr]]), and a phone counts steps well enough to follow a trend (inference).

**What a wrist band does well.** Steps come from an accelerometer. Optical heart rate reads blood-volume pulses through the skin: clean at rest, noisier when the wrist moves or grips a bar [@Bent2020_PPGinaccuracy]. Resting heart rate is worth tracking as a slow trend: each 10 bpm higher was associated with 17% higher all-cause mortality (RR 1.17, 48 studies) [@Aune2017_RHRmeta]; in these observational data it is a marker, partly of fitness, not a proven cause.

**What it does badly.** Energy expenditure is modelled, not measured, so device calories must never set your intake ([[dec:D04]]). Sleep stages are rough estimates [@Haghayegh2019_FitbitSleep], although bed and wake times are useful on your 04:00-12:00 schedule.

**Interval heart rate.** If you want it for the 4 x 4 sessions or the Rockport walk test ([[ex:test-rockport]]), a chest strap paired with your phone is the accurate option [@Gillinov2017_HRmonitors].
decisions.confidenceNote: The pattern (good steps and resting heart rate, poor calories and sleep stages) is consistent across reviews, but validation lags new models, so results for older devices may not transfer to the one you buy.

decisions.title: The aesthetic goal: feasibility and expectations
decisions.context: Your first priority is aesthetics: an athletic, not bulky look. A goal stated as a look, or as someone else's physique, cannot be measured, has no timeline and invites comparison with images whose conditions you cannot know. The programme needs an operational version of the goal and honest expectations about pace.

options.name: Operational goal on a multi-year horizon
options.summary: A lean athletic look defined by trends: shoulder-to-waist ratio rising, navel waist about 78-82 cm, strength and girths rising; a [[term:ffmi|fat-free mass index (FFMI)]] of 21-22 at a lean body-fat level as an illustration only.
options.for: In urban samples a V-shaped torso (low waist-to-chest ratio) was the main predictor of rated male attractiveness [@Swami2005_WCRcrossCultural], and rated strength explained over 70% of the variance in bodily attractiveness [@Sell2017_strengthAttractiveness]; both map onto girths you can measure.
options.against: These perception studies are cross-sectional, culturally limited and based on ratings of images, so they describe preferences, not what you will achieve.

options.name: Match a reference physique by a deadline
options.summary: Copy a chosen physique within, say, a year.
options.for: Concrete and motivating.
options.against: Responses vary enormously: biceps size change after identical training ranged from -2% to +59% [@Hubal2005_variability], and the average whole-body muscle gain over about 10 weeks was 1.53 kg [@Benito2020_wholeBodyHypertrophy]. The conditions behind any photographed physique cannot be known.

options.name: A single number
options.summary: A scale-weight or body-fat-percentage target.
options.for: Simple to state and check.
options.against: Weight cannot separate muscle from fat during recomposition, and circumference body-fat estimates were biased by about 4-6 percentage points against DXA [@McClung2025_CBEvsDXA], wider than the gap between 'lean' and 'very lean' (inference).

decisions.choiceSummary: Define the goal operationally (rising shoulder-to-waist ratio, navel waist about 78-82 cm, rising strength and girths) on a multi-year horizon, using FFMI 21-22 at a lean body-fat level only as an illustration of the destination.
decisions.rationale:
A measurable goal shows progress and can be adjusted; a picture does neither.

**Where you start.** At 181 cm, about 77 kg and an estimated 20% body fat (plausible 17-24%), your FFMI is about 18.8 kg/m² (plausible 17.9-19.5; arithmetic from your measurements), close to the median of 18.9 for men aged 18-34 [@Schutz2002_FFMIpercentiles].

**How far and how fast.** In one study drug-free men rarely exceeded a height-normalised FFMI of about 25, a finding its authors called preliminary [@Kouri1995_FFMI], and even in very large athletes muscle relative to height appears to plateau [@Abe2018_upperLimit]. FFMI 21-22 sits well inside that range: about 69-72 kg of [[term:ffm|fat-free mass]] at your height, roughly 7-10 kg more than your estimated 61.6 kg now (arithmetic, inference). With early gains of about 1.5 kg of muscle in 9-10 weeks [@Benito2020_wholeBodyHypertrophy], slowing with training age (inference), that is a multi-year project, and your own rate may be far from the average [@Hubal2005_variability].

**Size and perception.** Ratings showed no inverted U: the strongest-looking men were rated most attractive [@Sell2017_strengthAttractiveness], yet men overestimate the muscularity women prefer [@Lei2021_muscularityMisperception]. Neither supports chasing extreme size or fearing it. Becoming bulky by accident is unlikely for a drug-free novice (inference), and [[rule:size-control]] lets you hold a muscle group that gets ahead of the look you want. A navel waist of 78-82 cm also brings you to or near the 78 cm first action level proposed for Indian men in one study [@Misra2006_IndianWaist]. The programme compares you with no actor or public figure.
decisions.confidenceNote: Largely inference: the targets combine cross-sectional reference data, preliminary FFMI limits, short studies of novices and perception research from limited cultural samples.

decisions.title: Flexibility strategy for the toe-touch limitation
decisions.context: You cannot touch your toes with straight knees. Flexibility is in your lowest priority group, so the strategy must cost little time while still improving hamstring range, which also makes deep [[term:hip-hinge|hip-hinge]] and squat positions easier to reach.

options.name: Loaded full range plus cool-down stretching
options.summary: Romanian deadlifts and seated leg curls through full range as the main tool; hamstring static stretching in every cool-down, including the aerobic sessions (2 x 30 s per leg in 5-6 sessions a week, about 5-6 min per leg per week at about 7/10); an optional 5-min daily home routine; a monthly fingertip-to-floor test.
options.for: Resistance training improved [[term:rom|range of motion (ROM)]] (ES 0.73), more in untrained people (ES 1.04), and matched stretching [@Alizadeh2023_RT_ROM; @Afonso2021_STvsStretchMeta]. Weekly stretching time of at least about 5 min was associated with ROM gains [@Thomas2018_stretch_dose_ROM].
options.against: No pooled comparison shows that combining the two beats either alone: resistance training plus stretching equalled stretching alone (ES -0.001) [@Alizadeh2023_RT_ROM].

options.name: Stretching only
options.summary: A dedicated stretching programme as the main tool.
options.for: Stretch training increased ROM with an effect size of about 1.0 [@Konrad2024_chronic_stretch_ROM].
options.against: No better than resistance training for ROM [@Afonso2021_STvsStretchMeta], and it builds none of the muscle you are training for.

options.name: PNF stretching
options.summary: Contract-relax [[term:pnf|PNF]] stretching instead of static holds.
options.for: PNF and static stretching gave larger gains than ballistic or dynamic stretching [@Konrad2024_chronic_stretch_ROM].
options.against: In another dataset static protocols outperformed PNF [@Thomas2018_stretch_dose_ROM]; PNF usually needs a partner, and you train alone (practical convention).

options.name: Resistance training alone
options.summary: Rely on full-range lifting; no stretching.
options.for: Similar pooled ROM gain to stretching, at no extra time [@Alizadeh2023_RT_ROM].
options.against: Part of the toe-touch limit is tolerance of end-range stretch, which direct stretching trains [@Magnusson1996_stretch_tolerance], so dropping it gives up a cheap second route (inference).

decisions.choiceSummary: Use full-range loaded hamstring work (Romanian deadlift, seated leg curl) as the main tool, add hamstring static stretching to every cool-down, offer an optional 5-minute daily home routine, and re-test fingertip-to-floor monthly.
decisions.rationale:
Loading and stretching both increase range, and combining them costs only a few minutes a session.

**Mechanism.** Short-term gains from [[term:static-stretching|static stretching]] come mainly from higher [[term:stretch-tolerance|stretch tolerance]]: after 3 weeks of hamstring stretching in a small study of 7 adults, stiffness at a fixed angle was unchanged while the tolerated angle and torque rose [@Magnusson1996_stretch_tolerance]. In a calf study, stretching at 6-7/10 discomfort also cut muscle stiffness (57% vs 24% at low intensity) [@Nakamura2021_HI_vs_LI_SS]. Loaded work at long muscle lengths, such as the [[ex:db-rdl|Romanian deadlift]] and [[ex:seated-leg-curl|seated leg curl]], trains the same end range under tension. Part of a straight-leg limit may be neural: nerve-directed stretching raised ankle range by 9.9° by lowering sciatic-nerve stiffness [@Andrade2020_muscle_nerve_stretching]; its relevance to your toe-touch is inference.

**Dose and placement.** About 5 min per leg per week, spread over sessions, matches the dose associated with gains in one review [@Thomas2018_stretch_dose_ROM]. The stretch sits in the cool-down for range, not recovery: post-exercise stretching did not reduce soreness or speed strength recovery [@Afonso2021_postexercise_stretch_recovery].

**Measuring it.** In back-pain patients, the fingertip-to-floor test was valid (r -0.96 against radiographic trunk flexion), reliable (ICC 0.99) and responsive [@Perret2001_fingertip_floor_test], so a monthly [[ex:test-ftf]] is enough.
decisions.confidenceNote: Several meta-analyses agree that stretching and resistance training both improve ROM, but dose findings conflict (one meta-analysis found no moderation by volume or intensity [@Konrad2024_chronic_stretch_ROM]) and the neural share of your limit is unknown.

decisions.title: Balance asymmetry: single-leg work, left side first
decisions.context: Your left leg balances worse than your right: 20 vs 30 s with eyes open and 10 vs 15 s with eyes closed. Balance is in your lowest priority group, but single-leg control matters for lunges and split squats now and for running and jumping later. How much time should it get, and how should the gap be read?

options.name: Brief practice in warm-ups, left first
options.summary: 2 x 30 s of single-leg stance per leg in each warm-up, left side first; unilateral lower-body exercises started with the left leg; a standardised re-test each month.
options.for: Balance training improves the trained task (SMD 0.79, 95% CI 0.48-1.10) [@Kummel2016_specificity], so practising the stance you test is the most direct route; unilateral training improves unilateral strength more than bilateral training does (ES 0.65) [@Kassiano2025_uniVsBiMeta].
options.against: The weekly dose is far below the most effective dose in the dose-response meta-analysis [@Lesinski2015_balanceDR], so progress may be slower.

options.name: Dedicated balance programme
options.summary: Separate balance sessions at the 'optimal' dose.
options.for: The most effective parameters for steady-state balance were 11-12 weeks, 3 sessions a week and 11-15 min per session; untrained people improved with ES 0.82 [@Lesinski2015_balanceDR].
options.against: About 35-45 min a week for a low-priority goal, and the gains stay specific to the tasks trained [@Kummel2016_specificity].

options.name: Unstable-surface training
options.summary: Wobble boards, foam pads or similar.
options.for: A varied challenge that improves balance on the surface you train on (inference from task specificity).
options.against: Balance gains did not transfer meaningfully to untrained tasks, even similar ones (SMD -0.07 to 0.18) [@Kummel2016_specificity]; no catalogued trial shows that unstable-surface work improves stance on a stable floor.

options.name: Ignore it
options.summary: No specific balance work.
options.for: Healthy people's dominant and non-dominant legs perform the same on average [@Schorderet2021_dominance], so part of your gap may be test noise.
options.against: For the same reason, a gap that persists under standard testing is larger than expected, and your eyes-open times are well below the norm for men aged 18-39 (best of 3: 44.4 s) [@Springer2007_unipedalstance]; the fix costs about 2 minutes a session.

decisions.choiceSummary: Practise single-leg stance (2 x 30 s per leg) in every warm-up starting with the left leg, start unilateral lower-body exercises with the left leg, and re-test both legs monthly with a standard protocol, expecting gains mainly on the practised task.
decisions.rationale:
Practise the task you want to improve, a little and often, and let unilateral strength work do the rest.

**Read the gap first.** The norms use a strict protocol: barefoot, arms crossed, 45 s maximum, best of 3 trials [@Springer2007_unipedalstance]. Your baseline may not have followed it, so the first standardised [[ex:test-sls]] sets the real starting point. Your eyes-closed times (10 and 15 s) sit within the wide normal range for men aged 18-39 (16.9 ± 13.9 s) [@Springer2007_unipedalstance]; the eyes-open times are the clearer shortfall.

**Mechanism.** Single-leg stance integrates [[term:proprioception|proprioception]], vision and vestibular input into small ankle and hip corrections, and practice tunes that control for the practised task. Gains are specific: the trained task improved while untrained tasks barely changed [@Kummel2016_specificity]. Expect your stance times to rise; do not expect automatic transfer to running or sport.

**Left first.** Starting [[term:unilateral|unilateral]] sets on the weaker side gives it your freshest effort and lets it set the rep target for the right (practical convention). [[ex:bal-sls]] in the warm-up and [[ex:split-squat]], [[ex:reverse-lunge]] and [[ex:sl-rdl]] in training carry the work.
decisions.confidenceNote: Specificity and dose findings come from low-certainty meta-analyses, and whether your asymmetry is real or partly test noise is unknown until a standardised re-test.

decisions.title: Recovery tools: what to use and what to avoid
decisions.context: Ice baths, massage guns, foam rollers and compression garments are widely marketed for recovery. You are a novice whose top priority is muscle growth, training alone on a fixed budget, so a tool is worth using only if it does not blunt adaptation and gives a benefit you would notice.

options.name: Basics first; tools optional for comfort
options.summary: No regular cold-water immersion after lifting; massage or foam rolling optional for comfort; no compression garments; sleep, nutrition and sensible progression as the main levers.
options.for: The basics probably carry the largest effects (inference): in a small trial, one night without sleep cut [[term:mps|muscle protein synthesis (MPS)]] by 18% [@Lamon2021_sleepDeprivationMPS], and 6 h of sleep or less reduced performance by about 7.6% [@Craven2022_sleepLossPerformanceMA].
options.against: You give up the small reductions in [[term:doms|delayed-onset muscle soreness (DOMS)]] that several tools provide [@Dupuy2018_recovery_techniques_meta].

options.name: Regular cold-water immersion
options.summary: Cold-water immersion after most lifting sessions.
options.for: Water immersion and cryotherapy reduced DOMS and markers of muscle damage [@Dupuy2018_recovery_techniques_meta].
options.against: In one trial in 21 active men, muscle mass and strength rose more with active recovery than with cold water, and type II fibre area (+17%) increased only with active recovery [@Roberts2015_CWI_RT_adaptation]; pooled data favour no immersion for hypertrophy (posterior probability of a negative effect 0.957) [@Pinero2024_CWI_hypertrophy_meta] and show smaller strength gains (ES -0.23) [@Grgic2023_CWI_strength_meta].

options.name: Massage, foam rolling or compression as routine
options.summary: A recovery routine after every session.
options.for: Massage was the most effective method for DOMS and perceived fatigue [@Dupuy2018_recovery_techniques_meta]; foam rolling after exercise reduced perceived muscle pain (g 0.47) [@Wiewelhove2019_foam_rolling_meta].
options.against: Massage did not improve strength, jump, sprint or endurance [@Davis2020_massage_meta]; foam-rolling effects were minor overall [@Wiewelhove2019_foam_rolling_meta]; compression had no strength-sparing effect at any time point [@Negyesi2022_compression_meta].

options.name: Long cool-down or stretching for recovery
options.summary: An extended active cool-down or post-session stretching to speed recovery.
options.for: Active cool-downs speed blood lactate clearance [@VanHooren2018_cooldown].
options.against: They are largely ineffective for next-day performance and soreness [@VanHooren2018_cooldown], and stretching reduced soreness by a clinically trivial amount [@Herbert2011_Cochrane_stretch_DOMS].

decisions.choiceSummary: Avoid regular cold-water immersion after lifting, treat massage and foam rolling as optional comfort measures, skip compression garments, and rely on sleep, nutrition and sensible progression for recovery.
decisions.rationale:
Recovery for a novice is mostly about not undermining adaptation and letting your own repair processes work.

**Why cold water is avoided.** Growth depends on the signalling that follows each session. In a small biopsy study (mechanistic data), cold-water immersion after lifting blunted the rise in Pax7+ [[term:satellite-cells|satellite cells]] and the phosphorylation of p70S6K, a downstream target of [[term:mtorc1|mTORC1]], over 2-48 h [@Roberts2015_CWI_RT_adaptation]. Limb-only immersion attenuated strength gains (ES -0.31), while whole-body immersion showed no clear difference (ES -0.08, wide interval) [@Grgic2023_CWI_strength_meta]. An ordinary cool shower in hot weather is not what these trials tested (inference).

**Why soreness is not the target.** DOMS peaks in your first weeks and fades through the [[term:repeated-bout-effect|repeated-bout effect]], which the gentle start in [[dec:D07]] relies on. Massage and foam rolling can make you feel better and are fine if you enjoy them, but they restore performance little if at all [@Davis2020_massage_meta; @Wiewelhove2019_foam_rolling_meta]. The cool-down stretch is there for range, not recovery ([[dec:D27]]).

**The real levers.** Protect the sleep window ([[dec:D22]]), meet your protein target ([[dec:D19]]), progress gradually ([[dec:D09]]) and take a [[rule:deload]] when fatigue accumulates.
decisions.confidenceNote: The case against routine cold water rests on one well-controlled trial and two low-certainty meta-analyses that agree in direction; evidence on massage, foam rolling and compression is low certainty but consistently shows small, mostly subjective effects.
